When you declare a class to be public, you must declare the class in a file whose name is exactly the same as the name of the class (but with the .java extension added). For example, if you declare public class MyImportantCode, you must put the class's code in a file named MyImportantCode.java, with uppercase letters M, I, and C and all other letters lowercase. This file-naming rule has an important consequence: If your code declares two public classes, your code must consist of at least two .java files. In other words, you can't declare two public classes in one .java file.

For more news about the word public and other such words, see Chapter 11.

PLAYING THE LONG GAME

Rewrite the first listing in Chapter 5 (this book's first Guessing Game example) in the style of Listing 7-11. (If you can, test your code in an environment that runs Java 20 or earlier.)

Experiments with Variables

One summer during my college days, I was sitting on the front porch, loafing around and talking with someone I'd just met. I think her name was Janine. “Where are you from?” I asked. “Mars,” she answered. She paused to see whether I'd ask a follow-up question.

As it turned out, Janine was from Mars, Pennsylvania, a small town about 20 miles north of Pittsburgh. Okay, what’s my point? The point is that the meaning of a name depends on the context. If you’re just north of Pittsburgh and ask, “How do I get to Mars from here?” you may receive a sensible, nonchalant answer. But if you ask the same question standing on a street corner in Manhattan, you’ll probably arouse some suspicion. (Okay, knowing Manhattan, people would probably just ignore you.)

Of course, the people who live in Mars, Pennsylvania, are very much aware that their town has an oddball name. Fond memories of teenage years at Mars High School don’t prevent a person from knowing about the big red planet. On a clear evening in August, you can still have the following conversation with one of the local residents:

  • You: How do I get to Mars?
  • Local resident: You’re in Mars, pal. What particular part of Mars are you looking for?
  • You: No, I don’t mean Mars, Pennsylvania. I mean the planet Mars.
  • Local resident: Oh, the planet! Well, then, catch the 8:19 train leaving for Cape Canaveral. No, wait — that’s the local train. That’d take you through West Virginia … .

The meaning of a name depends on where you’re using the name. Although most English-speaking people think of Mars as a place with a carbon dioxide atmosphere, some folks in Pennsylvania think about all the shopping they can do in Mars. And those folks in Pennsylvania really have two meanings for the name Mars. In Java, those names may look like this: Mars and planets.Mars.

Putting a variable in its place

Your first experiment is shown in Listings 7-12 and 7-13. The listings' code highlights the difference between two kinds of variables:

  • Field: A variable that's not declared inside of a method.
  • Method-local variable: A variable that is declared inside of a method.

LISTING 7-12 Two Meanings for Mars

import java.io.IO;

class EnglishSpeakingWorld {
String mars = " red planet"; // field

void visitPennsylvania() {
IO.println("visitPA is running:");

String mars = " Janine's home town"; // method-local variable

IO.println(mars); // Janine's home town
IO.println(this.mars); // red planet
}
}

LISTING 7-13 Calling the Code of Listing 7-12

void main() {
println("main is running:");
var e = new EnglishSpeakingWorld();

//out.println(mars); cannot resolve symbol
println(e.mars);
e.visitPennsylvania();
}

Figure 7-11 shows a run of the code in Listings 7-12 and 7-13. Figure 7-12 shows a diagram of the code's structure. Notice that, in this example, I choose to put the main method outside of the EnglishSpeakingWorld class.

The main method creates an instance of the EnglishSpeakingWorld class. The variable e refers to the new instance. The new instance is an object with a variable named mars inside it. That mars variable has the value "red planet". This mars variable is a field.

Another way to describe that mars field is to call it an instance variable because that mars variable (the variable whose value is "red planet") belongs to an instance of the EnglishSpeakingWorld class.

Now look at the main method in Listing 7-13. Inside the main method, you aren't permitted to write println(mars). In other words, a bare-faced reference to any mars variable is a definite no-no. The mars variable that I mention in the preceding paragraph belongs to the EnglishSpeakingWorld class. But the main method lives outside of the EnglishSpeakingWorldClass. Too bad for that!

However, inside the main method, you can certainly write e.mars because the e variable refers to your EnglishSpeakingWorld object. That's nice.

Near the bottom of Listing 7-13, you call the visitPennsylvania method. When you're inside visitPennsylvania, you have another declaration of a mars variable, whose value is "Janine's home town". This particular mars variable is a method-local variable because it belongs to just one method: the visitPennsylvania method.

Now you have to worry about two variables in Listing 7-12, both with the name mars. One mars variable, a field, has the value "red planet". The other mars variable, a method-local variable, has the value "Janine's home town". In Listing 7-12, when you use the word mars, which of the two variables are you referring to?

The answer is, when you're visiting Pennsylvania, the variable with value "Janine's home town" wins. When in Pennsylvania, think the way the Pennsylvanians think. When you're executing code inside the visitPennsylvania method, resolve any variable name conflicts by going with method-local variables — variables declared right inside the visitPennsylvania method.

What if you're in Pennsylvania and need to refer to that 2-mooned celestial object? More precisely, how does code inside the visitPennsylvania method refer to the field with value "red planet"? The answer is, use this.mars. The word this points to whatever object contains all this code (and not to any methods inside the code). That object, an instance of the EnglishSpeakingWorld class, has a big, fat mars field, and that field's value is "red planet". So that's how you can force code to see outside the method it’s in — you use the Java keyword this.

For more information on the keyword this, see Chapter 10.

Telling a variable where to go

Years ago, when I lived in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, I made frequent use of the local bank's automatic teller machines. Machines of this kind were just beginning to become standardized. The local teller machine system was named TYME, which stood for Take Your Money Everywhere.

I remember traveling by car out to California. At one point, I got hungry and stopped for a meal, but I was out of cash. So I asked a gas station attendant, “Do you know where there's a TYME machine around here?”

So you see, a name that works well in one place could work terribly, or not at all, in another place. In Listings 7-14 and 7-15, I illustrate this point (with more than just an anecdote about teller machines).

LISTING 7-14 Tale of Atomic City

import java.io.IO;

class EnglishSpeakingWorld2 {
String mars;

void visitIdaho() {
IO.println("visitID is running:");

mars = " red planet";
String atomicCity = " Population: 25";

IO.println(mars);
IO.println(atomicCity);
}

void visitNewJersey() {
IO.println("visitNJ is running:");
IO.println(mars);
// IO.println(atomicCity); cannot resolve symbol
}
}

LISTING 7-15 Calling the Code of Listing 7-14

void main() {
var e = new EnglishSpeakingWorld2();

e.visitIdaho();
e.visitNewJersey();
}

Figure 7-13 shows a run of the code in Listings 7-14 and 7-15. Figure 7-14 shows a diagram of the code’s structure. The code for EnglishSpeakingWorld2 has two variables: The mars variable, which isn't declared inside a method, is a field; the other variable, atomicCity, is a method-local variable and is declared inside the visitIdaho method.

In Listing 7-14, notice where each variable can and can't be used. When you try to use the atomicCity variable inside the visitNewJersey method, you see an error message. Literally, the message says cannot resolve symbol. Figuratively, the message says, “Hey, buddy, Atomic City is in Idaho, not New Jersey.” Technically, the message says that the method-local variable atomicCity is available only in the visitIdaho method because that's where the variable was declared.

Back inside the visitIdaho method, you're free to use the atomicCity variable as much as you want. After all, the atomicCity variable is declared inside the visitIdaho method.

And what about Mars? Have you forgotten about your old friend, that lovely 80-degrees-below-0 planet? Well, both the visitIdaho and visitNewJersey methods can access the mars variable. That's because the mars variable is a field. That is, the mars variable is declared in the code for the EnglishSpeakingWorld2 class but not inside any particular method. (In my stories about the names for things, remember that people who live in both states, Idaho and New Jersey, have heard of the planet Mars.)

The life cycle of the mars field has three separate steps:

  1. When the EnglishSpeakingWorld2 class first flashes into existence, the computer sees String mars and creates space for the mars field.
  2. When the visitIdaho method is executed, the method assigns the value "red planet" to the mars field. (The visitIdaho method also prints the value of the mars field.)
  3. When the visitNewJersey method is executed, the method prints the mars value once again.

In this way, the mars field's value is passed from one method to another.

Try out these programs. See what you think.

WHO'S WHO?

What's the output of the following code? Why?

import java.io.IO;

public class Main1 {
String name = "Nancy";

void main() {
IO.println(name);
String name = "Barry";
IO.println(name);
}
}

WHO ELSE IS WHO?

What's the output of the following code? Why?

import java.io.IO;

public class Main2 {
String name = "George";

void main() {
doStuff();
}

void doStuff() {
IO.println(name);

String name = "Barry";
IO.println(name);

IO.println(this.name);
}
}

Passing Parameters

A method can communicate with another part of your Java program in several ways. One way is by way of the method's parameter list. Using a parameter list, you pass on-the-fly information to a method as the method is being called.

Imagine that the information you pass to the method is stored in one of your program’s variables. What, if anything, does the method actually do with that variable? The following sections present a few interesting case studies.

Pass by value

According to my web research, the town of Smackover, Arkansas, has 2,232 people in it. But my research isn’t current. Just yesterday, Dora Kermongoos celebrated a joyous occasion over at Smackover General Hospital — the birth of her healthy, brown-eyed baby girl. (The girl weighs 7 pounds, 4 ounces, and is 21 inches tall.) Now the town’s population has risen to 2,233.

Listing 7-16 has a very bad program in it. The program is supposed to add 1 to a variable that stores Smackover’s population, but the program doesn’t work. Take a look at Listing 7-16 to see why.

LISTING 7-16 This Program Doesn’t Work

void main() {
int smackoverARpop = 2232;

birth(smackoverARpop);
println(smackoverARpop);
}

void birth(int cityPop) {
cityPop++;
}

When you run the program in Listing 7-16, the program displays the number 2232 onscreen. After nine months of planning and anticipation and Dora’s whopping seven hours in labor, the Kermongoos family’s baby girl wasn’t registered in the system. What a shame!

The improper use of parameter passing caused the problem. In Java, when you pass a parameter that has one of the eight primitive types, that parameter is passed by value.

For a review of Java’s eight primitive types, see Chapter 4.

Here’s what this means in plain English: Any changes that the method makes to the value of its parameter don’t affect the values of variables back in the calling code. In Listing 7-16, the birth method can apply the ++ operator to cityPop all it wants — the application of ++ to the cityPop parameter has absolutely no effect on the value of the smackoverARpop variable back in the main method.

Technically, what's happening is the copying of a value. (See Figure 7-15.) When the main method calls the birth method, the value stored in smackoverARpop is copied to another memory location — a location reserved for the cityPop parameter's value. During the birth method's execution, 1 is added to the cityPop parameter. But the place where the original 2232 value was stored — the memory location for the smackoverARpop variable — remains unaffected.

When you do parameter passing with any of the eight primitive types, the computer uses pass by value. The value stored in the calling code's variable remains unchanged. This happens even if the calling code's variable and the called method’s parameter happen to have exactly the same name.

Returning a result

You must fix the problem that the code in Listing 7-16 poses. After all, a young baby Kermongoos can’t go through life untracked. To record this baby’s existence, you have to add 1 to the value of the smackoverARpop variable. You can do this in plenty of ways, and the way presented in Listing 7-17 isn’t the simplest. Even so, the way shown in Listing 7-17 illustrates a point: Returning a value from a method call can be an acceptable alternative to parameter passing. Look at Listing 7-17 to see what I mean.

LISTING 7-17 This Program Works

void main() {
int smackoverARpop = 2232;

smackoverARpop = birth(smackoverARpop);
println(smackoverARpop);
}

int birth(int cityPop) {
return cityPop + 1;
}

After running the code in Listing 7-17, the number you see on your computer screen is the correct number: 2233.

The code in Listing 7-17 has no new features in it (unless you call working correctly a new feature). The most important idea in Listing 7-17 is the return statement, which also appears in Chapter 7. Even so, Listing 7-17 presents a nice contrast to the approach in Listing 7-16, which had to be discarded.

Pass by reference

In the previous section or two, I take great pains to emphasize a certain point — that when a parameter has one of the eight primitive types, the parameter is passed by value. If you read this, you probably missed the emphasis on the parameter's having one of the eight primitive types. The emphasis is needed because passing objects (reference types) doesn't quite work the same way.

When you pass an object to a method, the object is passed by reference. What this means to you is that statements in the called method can change any values that are stored in the object’s variables. Those changes do affect the values that are seen by whatever code called the method. Listings 7-18 and 7-19 illustrate the point.

LISTING 7-18 What Is a City?

class City {
int population;
}

LISTING 7-19 Passing an Object to a Method

void main() {
var smackoverAR = new City();
smackoverAR.population = 2232;
birth(smackoverAR);
println(smackoverAR.population);
}

void birth(City aCity) {
aCity.population++;
}

When you run the code in Listings 7-18 and 7-19, the output you see is the number 2233. That’s good because the code has things like ++ and the word birth in it. The deal is, adding 1 to aCity.population inside the birth method actually changes the value of smackoverAR.population, as it's known in the main method.

To see how the birth method changes the value of smackoverAR.population, look at Figure 7-16. When you pass an object to a method, the computer doesn't make a copy of the entire object. Instead, the computer makes a copy of a reference to that object. (Think of it the way it's shown in Figure 7-16. The computer makes a copy of an arrow that points to the object.)

In Figure 7-16, you see just one instance of the City class, with a population variable inside it. Now keep your eye on that object as you read the following steps:

  1. Just before the birth method is called, the smackoverAR variable refers to that object — the instance of the City class.
  2. When the birth method is called and smackoverAR is passed to the birth method's aCity parameter, the computer copies the reference from smackoverAR to aCity. Now aCity refers to that same object — the instance of the City class.
  3. When the statement aCity.population++ is executed inside the birth method, the computer adds 1 to the object's population field. Now the program's one-and-only City instance has 2233 stored in its population field.
  4. The flow of execution goes back to the main method. The value of smackoverAR.population is printed. But smackoverAR refers to that one instance of the City class. So smackoverAR.population has the value 2233. The Kermongoos family is so proud.

Returning an object from a method

Believe it or not, the previous sections on parameter passing left unexplored one nook-and-cranny of Java methods: When you call a method, the method can return something right back to the calling code. In previous chapters and sections, I return primitive values, such as int values, or nothing (otherwise known as void). In this section, I return a whole object. It's an object of type City from Listing 7-18. The code that makes this happen is in Listing 7-20.

LISTING 7-20 Here, Have a City

void main() {
var smackoverAR = new City();
smackoverAR.population = 2232;
smackoverAR = doBirth(smackoverAR);
println(smackoverAR.population);
}

City doBirth(City aCity) {
var myCity = new City();
myCity.population = aCity.population + 1;
return myCity;
}

If you run the code in Listing 7-20, you get the number 2233. That's good. The code works by telling the doBirth method to create another City instance. In the new instance, the value of population is 2233. (See Figure 7-17.)

After the doBirth method is executed, that City instance is returned to the main method. Then, back in the main method, that instance (the one that doBirth returns) is assigned to the smackoverAR variable. (See Figure 7-18.) Now smackoverAR refers to a brand-new City instance — an instance whose population is 2,233.

In Listing 7-20, notice the type consistency in the calling and returning of the doBirth method:

  • The smackoverAR variable has type City. The smackoverAR variable is passed to the aCity parameter, which is also of type City.
  • The myCity variable is of type City. The myCity variable is sent back in the doBirth method's return statement. That's consistent, because the doBirth method's header begins with static City doBirth(blah, blah, blah… — a promise to return an object of type City.
  • The doBirth method returns an object of type City. Back in the main method, the object that the call to doBirth returns is assigned to the smackoverAR variable, and (you guessed it) the smackoverAR variable is of type City.

Aside from being quite harmonious, all this type agreement is absolutely necessary. If you write a program in which your types don't agree with one another, the compiler spits out an unsympathetic incompatible types message.

A final word

Dora Kermongoos and her newborn baby daughter are resting comfortably in their Smackover, Arkansas, home. Be sure to watch the upcoming reality television series, Smackover Newborns: Secrets from Behind Closed Doors.

Chapter 8

Constructing New Objects

IN THIS CHAPTER

Defining constructors

Using Java’s default constructor

Creating a class with one line of code

Ms. Jennie Burd

121 Schoolhouse Lane

Anywhere, Kansas

Dear Ms. Burd,

In response to your letter of June 21, I believe I can say with complete assurance that objects are not created spontaneously from nothing. Although I’ve never actually seen an object being created (and no one else in this office can claim to have seen an object in its moment of creation), I have every confidence that some process or another is responsible for the building of these interesting and useful thingamajigs. We here at ObjectsAndClasses.com support the unanimous opinions of both the scientific community and the private sector in matters of this nature. Furthermore, we agree with the recent finding of a blue-ribbon panel that concludes, beyond any doubt, that spontaneous object creation would impede the present economic outlook.

Please be assured that I have taken all steps necessary to ensure the safety and well-being of you, our loyal customer. If you have any further questions, please do not hesitate to contact our Complaint department. The department’s manager is Mr. Blake Wholl. You can contact him by visiting our company’s website.

Once again, let me thank you for your concern, and I hope you continue to patronize ObjectsAndClasses.com.

Yours truly,

Mr. Scott Brickenchicker (the one who couldn’t get on the elevator in Chapter 4)

Defining Constructors (What It Means to Be a Temperature)

Here’s a statement that creates an object:

Account myAccount = new Account();

I know it works — I got it from one of my own examples in Chapter 7. Anyway, Chapter 7 has me saying, “When Java performs the initialization myAccount = new Account(), Java creates a new object (a new instance of the Account class) and makes the variable myAccount refer to that new object.” What does this pithy sentence mean?

Well, the keyword new tells Java to create an object — an instance of a class. Java responds by performing certain actions. For starters, Java finds a place in its memory to store information about the new object. If the object has fields, the fields should eventually have meaningful values.

To find out about fields, see Chapter 7.

When you ask Java to create a new object, you may want to specify what's placed in the object's fields. And what if you’re interested in doing more than filling fields? Perhaps, when Java creates a new object, you have a whole list of jobs for Java to carry out. For instance, when Java creates a new window object, you want Java to realign the sizes of all buttons in that window.

Creating a new object can involve all kinds of tasks, so in this chapter you create constructors. A constructor tells Java to perform a new object’s start-up tasks.

What is a temperature?

“Good morning, and welcome to Object News. The local temperature in your area is a pleasant 73 degrees Fahrenheit.”

Each temperature consists of two parts: a number and a temperature scale. A number is just a double value, such as 32.0 or 70.52. But what's a temperature scale? Is it a string of characters, like "Fahrenheit" or "Celsius"? Not really, because some strings aren't temperature scales. There's no "Quelploof" temperature scale, and a program that can display the temperature "73 degrees Quelploof" is a bad program. So how can you limit the temperature scales to the small number of scales that people use? One way to do it is with Java's enum type.

What is a temperature scale? (Java's enum type)

Java provides lots of ways for you to group things together. In Chapter 12, you group things to form an array. And in Chapter 12, you group things to form a collection. In this chapter, you group things into an enum type. (Of course, you can't group anything unless you can pronounce enum. The word enum is pronounced “ee-NOOM,” like the first two syllables of the word enumeration.)

Creating a complicated enum type isn't easy, but to create a simple enum type, just write a bunch of words inside a pair of curly braces. Listing 8-1 defines an enum type. The name of the enum type is TempScale.

LISTING 8-1 The TempScale Type (an enum Type)

public enum TempScale {
CELSIUS, FAHRENHEIT, KELVIN, RANKINE
}

(Author's note: In Listing 8-1, I list four different temperature scales. In previous Java For Dummies editions, I tried to show off by listing nine temperature scales, some with fancy Unicode characters in their names. But during my research for this edition, I stumbled upon www.curiousnotions.com/temperature-converter a website with formulas for 73 different temperature scales. I am truly humbled.)

When you define an enum type, two important things happen:

  • You create values.

    Just as 13 and 151 are int values, CELSIUS and FAHRENHEIT are TempScale values.

  • You can create variables to refer to those values.

    In Listing 8-2, I declare the fields number and scale. Just as

    double number;

    declares that a number variable is of type double,

    TempScale scale;

    declares variable scale to be of type TempScale.

    “To be of type TempScale” means that you can have values CELSIUS, FAHRENHEIT, KELVIN, or RANKINE. So, in Listing 8-2, I can give the scale variable the value FAHRENHEIT (or TempScale.FAHRENHEIT, to be more precise).

An enum type is a Java class in disguise. That's why Listing 8-1 contains an entire file devoted to one thing — namely, the declaration of an enum type (the TempScale type). Like the declaration of a class, an enum type declaration belongs in a file all its own. The code in Listing 8-1 belongs in a file named TempScale.java.

Okay, so then what is a temperature?

Each temperature consists of two things: a number and a temperature scale. The code in Listing 8-2 makes this fact abundantly clear.

LISTING 8-2 The Temperature Class

public class Temperature {
private double number;

private TempScale scale;

public Temperature() {
number = 0.0;
scale = TempScale.FAHRENHEIT;
}

public Temperature(double number) {
this.number = number;
scale = TempScale.FAHRENHEIT;
}

public Temperature(TempScale scale) {
number = 0.0;
this.scale = scale;
}

public Temperature(double number, TempScale scale) {
this.number = number;
this.scale = scale;
}

public void setNumber(double number) {
this.number = number;
}

public double getNumber() {
return number;
}

public void setScale(TempScale scale) {
this.scale = scale;
}

public TempScale getScale() {
return scale;
}

public String toString() {
return String.format("%5.2f\u00B0 ", number) + scale;
}
}

The code in Listing 8-2 has the usual setter and getter methods (accessor methods for the number and scale fields).

For some good reading on setter and getter methods (also known as accessor methods), see Chapter 7.

SEE THE FOREST FOR THE TREES

Listing 8-2 is a whopping 35 lines long, not counting the blank lines. Despite its length the code in Listing 8-2 is pretty boring. The code follows the recommended practice of making a class's fields private. (Refer to Chapter 7.) Since number and scale are private, Listing 8-2 has to include setter and getter methods. If you don't bother to make the fields private, you don't need these setters and getters, so Listing 8-2 becomes shorter, like this:

public class Temperature {
double number;

TempScale scale;

public Temperature() {
number = 0.0;
scale = TempScale.FAHRENHEIT;
}

public Temperature(double number) {
this.number = number;
scale = TempScale.FAHRENHEIT;
}

public Temperature(TempScale scale) {
number = 0.0;
this.scale = scale;
}

public Temperature(double number, TempScale scale) {
this.number = number;
this.scale = scale;
}

public String toString() {
return String.format("%5.2f\u00B0 ", number) + scale;
}
}

In fact, when I look at Listing 8-2, this is what I see:

public class Temperature {
double number;

TempScale scale;

/*
* Four constructors belong here.
* Note to self: Tell readers what a constructor
* is in the sections to follow.
*/

public String toString() {
return String.format("%5.2f\u00B0 ", number) + scale;
}
}

That's the right way to think about code. Focus on the broad outline. Zoom in on the details after you've taken in the big picture.

In addition to its setters and getters, Listing 8-2 has four other method-like-looking things. Each of these method-like things has the name Temperature, which happens to be the same as the name of the class. None of these Temperature method-like things has a return type of any kind — not even void, which is the cop-out return type.

Each of these method-like things is called a constructor. A constructor is like a method, except that a constructor has a special purpose: to create new objects.

Whenever the computer creates a new object, the computer executes the statements inside a constructor.

What you can do with a temperature

Listing 8-3 gives form to some of the ideas that I describe in the preceding section. In Listing 8-3, you call the constructors that are declared earlier, in Listing 8-2. Figure 8-1 shows what happens when you run all this code.

LISTING 8-3 Using the Temperature Class

public class UseTemperature {

public static void main(String[] args) {

var temp = new Temperature();
temp.setNumber(70.0);
temp.setScale(TempScale.FAHRENHEIT);
System.out.println(temp);

temp = new Temperature(32.0);
System.out.println(temp);

temp = new Temperature(TempScale.CELSIUS);
System.out.println(temp);

temp = new Temperature(2.73, TempScale.KELVIN);
System.out.println(temp);
}
}

In Listing 8-3, I use the traditional style for writing a main method with the method inside an explicit class. Code of this kind doesn't implicitly import the java.io.IO package's print, println, and readln methods. (Refer to Chapter 7.) So, Listing 8-3 makes a long-winded System.out.println call.

MORE FOREST; FEWER TREES

The last section of Chapter 7 describes two kinds of main methods — Java's traditional main methods and the newfangled, easy-to-read main methods in simple source files. A traditional main method looks like the one in Listing 8-3:

public class UseTemperature {

public static void main(String[] args) {

// Yada, yada, …
System.out.println(temp);

// Blah, blah, blah, …
}
}

When you see a traditional main method, don't get bogged down thinking about the extra text. When all is said and done, the code in Listing 8-3 is almost the same as its simpler main method cousin:

void main() {
var temp = new Temperature();
temp.setNumber(70.0);
temp.setScale(TempScale.FAHRENHEIT);
println(temp);

temp = new Temperature(32.0);
println(temp);

temp = new Temperature(TempScale.CELSIUS);
println(temp);

temp = new Temperature(2.73, TempScale.KELVIN);
println(temp);
}

There are a few programming pitfalls that may arise when you change from a simple source file to a traditional, long-winded main method. But life is short, so it's better not to worry about those pitfalls. Of course, if you really want to worry, you can skip to the discussion of Java static keyword in Chapter 11.

In Listing 8-3, each statement of the kind

temp = new Temperature(blah-blah);

calls one of the constructors from Listing 8-2. So, by the time the code in Listing 8-3 finishes running, it creates four instances of the Temperature class. Each instance is created by calling a different constructor from Listing 8-2.

In Listing 8-3, the last of the four constructor calls has two parameters: 2.73 and TempScale.KELVIN. This isn't particular to constructor calls. A method call or a constructor call can have a bunch of parameters. You separate one parameter from another with a comma. Another name for “a bunch of parameters” is a parameter list.

The only rule you must follow is to match the parameters in the call with the parameters in the declaration. For example, in Listing 8-3, the fourth and last constructor call

new Temperature(2.73, TempScale.KELVIN)

has two parameters: the first of type double and the second of type TempScale. Java approves of this constructor call because Listing 8-2 contains a matching declaration. That is, the header

public Temperature(double number, TempScale scale)

has two parameters: the first of type double and the second of type TempScale. If a Temperature constructor call in Listing 8-3 had no matching declaration in Listing 8-2, Listing 8-3 would crash and burn. (To state things more politely, Java would display errors when you tried to compile the code in Listing 8-3.)

What does a temperature look like?

The last item in Listing 8-2 is a toString method. When you call a print or println method, the first thing Java does is to call toString on your behalf. That way, whatever you're trying to display gets turned into a string of characters — a string that can show up on a computer screen. For example, when you call println(2 + 2), Java adds 2 and 2 to get the int value 4, then it changes the int value 4 into the string "4", and finally, Java displays the contents of that "4" string on the screen.

Every class has a toString method, whether you write code for it or not. If you remove the toString declaration from Listing 8-2, Java adds a toString method behind the scenes. I think of this added method as an implicit toString method. But, for reasons that become clear in Chapter 10, this added method is called the inheritedtoString method.

For most classes, the inherited toString method isn't user-friendly. To show you what I mean, I removed my toString declaration from Listing 8-2. Then I ran the code in Listing 8-3. This was the output:

Temperature@5b480cf9
Temperature@6f496d9f
Temperature@723279cf
Temperature@10f87f48

My Temperature class's inherited toString method isn't helpful at all. So, in Listing 8-2, I create my own toString method with the format string "%5.2f\u00B0 ". In this string, \u00B0 is the Unicode representation of a temperature's degree symbol (°).

For some wise remarks about Unicode, refer to Chapter 5.

Constructing a temperature; a slow-motion replay

When the computer executes one of the new Temperature statements in Listing 8-3, Java has to decide which of the constructors in Listing 8-2 to use. Java decides by looking at the parameter list — the stuff in parentheses after the words new Temperature. For instance, when the computer executes

temp = new Temperature(32.0);

from Listing 8-3, Java says to itself, “The number 32.0 in parentheses is a double value. One of the Temperature constructors in Listing 8-2 has just one parameter with type double. The constructor's header looks like this:

public Temperature(double number)

“So I guess I'll execute the statements inside that particular constructor.” Java goes on to execute the following statements:

this.number = number;
scale = TempScale.FAHRENHEIT;

As a result, you get a brand-new object whose number field has the value 32.0 and whose scale field has the value TempScale.FAHRENHEIT.

In the two lines of code, you have two statements that set values for the fields number and scale. Take a look at the second of these statements, which is a bit easier to understand. The second statement sets the new object's scale field to TempScale.FAHRENHEIT. You see, the constructor's parameter list is (double number), and that list doesn't include a scale value. So whoever programmed this code had to make a decision about what value to use for the scale field. The programmer could have chosen FAHRENHEIT or CELSIUS, but they could also have chosen KELVIN or RANKINE. (This programmer happens to live in New Jersey, in the United States, where people commonly use the old Fahrenheit temperature scale.)

Marching back to the first of the two statements, this first statement assigns a value to the new object's number field. The statement uses a cute trick that you can see in many constructors (and in other methods that assign values to objects' fields). To understand the trick, take a look at Listing 8-4. The listing shows you two ways that I could have written the same constructor code.

LISTING 8-4 Two Ways to Accomplish the Same Thing

//Use this constructor …

public Temperature(double whatever) {
number = whatever;
scale = TempScale.FAHRENHEIT;
}

// … or use this constructor …

public Temperature(double number) {
this.number = number;
scale = TempScale.FAHRENHEIT;
}

// … but don't put both constructors in your code.

Listing 8-4 has two constructors in it. In the first constructor, I use two different names: number and whatever. In the second constructor, I don't need two names. Rather than make up a new name for the constructor's parameter, I reuse an existing name by writing this.number.

Here’s what’s going on in Listing 8-2:

  • In the statement this.number = number, the name this.number refers to the new object's number field — the field that's declared near the top of Listing 8-2. (See Figure 8-2.)
  • In the statement this.number = number, number (on its own, without this) refers to the constructor's parameter. (Again, see Figure 8-2.)

WHAT'S THIS ALL ABOUT?

Suppose that your code contains a constructor — the first of the two constructors in Listing 8-4. The whatever parameter is passed a number like 32.0, for instance. Then the first statement in the constructor’s body assigns that value, 32.0, to the new object's number field. The code works. But in writing this code, you had to make up a new name for a parameter — the name whatever. And the only purpose for this new name is to hand a value to the object's number field. What a waste! To distinguish between the parameter and the number field, you gave a name to something that was just momentary storage for the number value.

Making up names is an art, not a science. I've gone through plenty of naming phases. Years ago, whenever I needed a new name for a parameter, I picked a confusing misspelling of the original variable name. (I'd name the parameter something like numbr or nuhmber.) I've also tried changing a variable name's capitalization to come up with a parameter name. (I’d use parameter names like Number or nUMBER.) In Chapter 7, I use 1-letter variable names such as a for an address and b for an account's balance. None of these naming schemes works well — I can never remember the quirky new names I've created. The good news is that this parameter-naming effort isn't necessary. You can give the parameter the same name as the variable. To distinguish between the two, you use the Java keyword this.

In general, this.someName refers to a field belonging to the object that contains the code. In contrast, plain old someName refers to the closest place where someName happens to be declared. In the statement this.number = number (refer to Listing 8-2), that closest place happens to be the Temperature constructor's parameter list.

The default constructor

The Temperature class declaration in Listing 8-2 has four constructors, each with its own parameter list. What happens if you don't include all four of them? The answer isn't as straightforward as you may think. To find out what happens, try this three-step experiment:

  1. Delete all four constructors from Listing 8-2. Then try to run the code in Listing 8-3.

    To get Listing 8-3 running, you have to delete three of the code's constructor calls. The only call that works is the parameterless new Temperature() call. When you don't declare any constructors, Java creates one for you. This implicit constructor has no parameters. It's called a default constructor.

    Look back at the Account class in Chapter 7. In that chapter, you don't declare any constructors. And yet, you're able to call new Account() in each of the chapter's main methods. That's Java's default constructor at work!

    Java's default constructor is an implicit element. For some exciting reading about implicit elements, refer to Chapter 5.

  2. Delete three of the four constructors from Listing 8-2. The only constructor that you don't delete is the parameterless constructor.

    When you do this, you get the same result as the one in Step 1. You don't have to let Java create an implicit default constructor for you. You can declare the parameterless constructor explicitly in your code. It's your choice.

  3. Delete three of the four constructors from Listing 8-2. The only constructor that you don't delete is the 2-parameter constructor Temperature(double number, TempScale scale).

    I call this the class's fully parameterized constructor. It's the constructor whose parameters include every one of the class's fields.

    When you eliminate all but the Temperature class's fully parameterized constructor, you can call new Temperature(2.73, TempScale.KELVIN), but you can't call new Temperature(). Why not? What happened to Java's wonderful default constructor?

    The rule for constructors is as follows: When you declare a class and you don't explicitly declare any constructors (as in Step 1), Java creates a parameterless default constructor on your behalf. But, when you declare any constructors in your code, Java doesn't create a default constructor. So, if you want your class to have a parameterless constructor and some other constructors, you have to declare all of them (including the parameterless constructor) in your code. Pretty strange, hey!

If you find this default constructor business confusing, you can avoid thinking about it. Instead of worrying about this section's experiments, just make sure to explicitly declare all the constructors you plan to call. If you plan to call a parameterless constructor, write code for it in your class declaration. If you plan to call any parameterized constructors (fully parameterized or not), write code for these constructors in your class declaration.

Finally, if you don't enjoy writing constructor definitions as much as I do, let your IDE do the work. From your IDE's main menu, try choosing Code ⇒   Generate ⇒   Constructor or Source ⇒   Generate Constructor.

The terminology can be confusing. Java has default constructors and inherited methods. Both of these things appear magically when you don't explicitly define them in your code. Fortunately, you can write programs without remembering that one is called default and the other is called inherited. All you have to do is understand what's going on when you read these words.

There's always more stuff for you to try.

SCHOOL DAYS

Create a Student class with a name, an ID number, a grade point average (GPA), and a major area of study. The student's name is a String. The student's ID number is an int value. The GPA is a double value between 0.0 and 4.0. The Major is an enum type, with values such as COMPUTER_SCIENCE, MATHEMATICS, LITERATURE, PHYSICS, and HISTORY.

Every student has a name and an ID number, but a brand-new student might not have a GPA or a major. Create constructors with and without GPA and Major parameters.

As usual, create a main method that makes use of your new Student class.

FLIGHT OF FANCY

Create an AirplaneFlight class with a flight number, a departure airport, the time of departure, an arrival airport, and a time of arrival. The flight number is an int value. The departure and arrival airport fields belong to an Airport enum type, with values corresponding to some of the official IATA airport codes. (For example, London Heathrow Airport's code is LHR; Los Angeles International Airport's code is LAX; check out www.iata.org/publications/Pages/code-search.aspx for a searchable database of airline codes.)

For the times of arrival and departure, use Java's LocalTime class. (For more on LocalTime, check out the LocalTime documents page at https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/time/LocalTime.html.) To create a LocalTime object that's set to 2:15 P.m. (also known as 14:15), execute

LocalTime twoFifteen = LocalTime.of(14, 15);

To create a LocalTime object that's set to the current time (according to the computer's system clock), execute

LocalTime currentTime = LocalTime.now();

Every flight has a number, a departure airport, and an arrival airport. But some flights might not have departure and arrival times. Create constructors with and without departure and arrival time parameters.

Create a main method that makes use of your new AirplaneFlight class.

The Easy Way to Create a Class

Listing 8-2 describes the Temperature class in about 40 lines of code. That's a lot of code to define something that has only two properties — a number and a temperature scale. Most of the code in Listing 8-2 is routine, boilerplate stuff. When my eyes rest on the statement this.number = number, my brain ignores it. A devilish voice inside me says, “Don't bother me with this.number = number. Tell me something I don't already know.” I don't expect to find anything interesting in a class declaration of this kind. So, if another programmer throws a curveball inside a class definition, I probably won't notice it. That's not good.

Maybe there's a better way to create a class. No, there isn't. I wrote this section just to complain about long class declarations.

Oops! I lied. There is a better way to create a class. Take a look at Listing 8-5.

LISTING 8-5 Your First Record Class

public record Temperature (double number, TempScale scale) {}

Listing 8-5 is about as small as any listing can be. And yet the code in Listing 8-5 completely defines a Temperature class. This Temperature class shares many features with the class in Listing 8-2 and even has a few features that Listing 8-2 lacks. The word record in Listing 8-5 makes this Temperature class be a special kind of class. To no one's surprise, it's called a record class. Every record class has certain characteristics that make life easy for Java programmers.

The code in Listing 8-6 creates instances of the record class in Listing 8-5. Figure 8-3 shows the output from Listings 8-5 and 8-6.

LISTING 8-6 Instances of a Record Class

void main() {

var temp = new Temperature(70.0, TempScale.FAHRENHEIT);
println(String.format("%5.2f\u00B0 ", temp.number()) + temp.scale());

temp = new Temperature(2.73, TempScale.KELVIN);
println(temp);
}

Listing 8-6 does more or less the same things that Listing 8-3 does. The listing creates some Temperature instances and displays them. But record classes march to the beat of their own drummers. So Listing 8-6 isn't quite the same as the original Listing 8-3.

For one thing, a record class doesn't implicitly create a parameterless default constructor. Instead, a record class implicitly creates a fully parameterized constructor. That's why, in Listing 8-6, you see these two lines:

var temp = new Temperature(70.0, TempScale.FAHRENHEIT);

temp = new Temperature(2.73, TempScale.KELVIN);

But you don't see any of these lines:

// Don't add any of these lines to Listing 8-6.
var temp = new Temperature();
temp.number = 21.0;
temp.scale = TempScale.CELSIUS;

temp.setNumber(70.0);
temp.setScale(TempScale.FAHRENHEIT);

This section's Temperature class doesn't let you call new Temperature() and doesn't let you set the values of an existing object's number or scale fields. Once you've created an object with new Temperature(70.0, TempScale.FAHRENHEIT), you can't change that object's number value from 70.0 to 71.5. You can't change the object's scale value, either.

The word immutability means “unchangeable,” and instances of record classes are all immutable. Contrary to popular opinion, immutability is a good thing. At least, the immutability of an object is a good thing. If an object's field values never change, you know what those values are from the creation of the object until the end of the program's run. Other programmers can't add code that changes values and fouls up your logic.

But remember — this immutability business doesn't apply to variables that refer to record class instances. Look at the temp variable in Listing 8-6. During a run of this code, the temp variable refers to two different objects. One is a comfortable room temperature, and the other is the temperature of our chilly cosmic microwave background. In Listing 8-6, there's nothing to keep you from changing the object that temp refers to. But once you've created an object, that object's fields can't be changed.

What if you want to print a Temperature instance's number field? The expressions temp.number and temp.getNumber() won't work. But you can follow the pattern in the first println call of Listing 8-6. You can refer to temp.number() and temp.scale(). You type the name of the field followed by an empty pair of parentheses. That's the way you get the value of a record class's field.

This differs from the conventions for classes that aren't record classes, so you have to be careful. (And I have to be careful. I've gotten this wrong many times.)

The last line in Figure 8-3 shows what you get when you don't explicitly format a record class instance. Java quietly concocts a decent-looking toString method. You don't see that toString method in your code. But, when you call println(temp) in Listing 8-6, Java displays the temp object's number and scale values. (Refer to Figure 8-3.) That's good!

Listing 8-5 shows you how to define a class with only one line of code. Impressive as that is, you may want to create a record class that includes some customized method declarations. Listing 8-7 adds the toString method to a Temperature record class.

LISTING 8-7 Another Record Class

public record Temperature (double number, TempScale scale) {

public String toString() {
return String.format("%5.2f\u00B0 ", number) + scale;
}
}

With the toString method in Listing 8-7, a call to println(temp) displays a nicely formatted Fahrenheit room temperature. Figure 8-4 shows you what you get when you run the main method in Listing 8-6 against the Temperature class in Listing 8-7.

Constructors don't have to be dull

Here's a quote from somewhere near the start of this chapter: “… what if you’re interested in doing more than filling fields? Perhaps, when the computer creates a new object, you have a whole list of jobs for the computer to carry out.” Okay, what-if?

With the Temperature classes in previous sections, a programmer can create temperatures that are colder than absolute zero. And, in physics, that's a definite no-no. Listing 8-8 has a constructor that makes this science fiction scenario impossible.

LISTING 8-8 It's Cold Outside!

public record Temperature(double number, TempScale scale) {

public Temperature(double number, TempScale scale) {

this.number = Math.max(number,
switch (scale) {
case CELSIUS -> -273.15;
case FAHRENHEIT -> -459.6;
case KELVIN, RANKINE -> 0.0;
}
);
this.scale = scale;
}

public String toString() {
return String.format("%5.2f\u00B0 ", number) + scale;
}
}

When you use Listing 8-8 and run the following main method, you get the result shown in Figure 8-5.

void main() {
println(new Temperature(-1000.0, TempScale.FAHRENHEIT));

println(new Temperature(-1000.0, TempScale.CELSIUS));

println(new Temperature(-1000.0, TempScale.KELVIN));

println(new Temperature(2.73, TempScale.KELVIN));
}

In Listing 8-8, the max method (a member of Java's Math class) returns the larger of two numbers. For example, when number is –1000.00 and scale is FAHRENHEIT, the switch expression in Listing 8-8 returns –459.6. So this.number becomes Math.max(-1000.00, -459.6), which is -459.6. The new object's temperature is the lowest it can possibly be, and no lower. (Just writing about it makes me want to bundle up!)

ENUM TYPES AND SWITCHES

Listings 8-2 and 8-3 contain long-winded names such as TempScale.FAHRENHEIT and TempScale.CELSIUS. Names such as FAHRENHEIT and CELSIUS belong to my TempScale type (the type defined in Listing 8-1). These names have no meaning outside of my TempScale context. (If you think I'm being egotistical with this “no meaning outside of my context” remark, try deleting the TempScale. part of TempScale.FAHRENHEIT in Listing 8-2. Suddenly, Java tells you that your code contains an error.)

Java is normally fussy about type names and dots. But when the stewards of Java created enum types, they decided that enum types in switch structures deserve special treatment. You can use an enum value to decide which case to use in a switch statement or switch expression. When you do this, you don't have to use the enum type name in the case expressions. For example, in Listing 8-8, the first case value is CELSIUS, not TempScale.CELSIUS.

In newer versions of Java, you can write CELSIUS or TempScale.CELSIUS inside a switch. But in older versions, you have to write the short name CELSIUS. The longer name TempScale.CELSIUS causes havoc in a switch structure's case.

Chapter 5 introduces two kinds of switch structures: the switch statement and the switch expression. A switch statement does something (such as print a message), and a switch expression has a value (such as -273.15). Java's rules for switch expressions differ slightly from the rules for switch statements.

Here's a perfectly good switch statement:

switch (scale) {
case CELSIUS -> println("degrees Celsius");
case FAHRENHEIT -> println("degrees Fahrenheit");
}

If the temp object's scale is KELVIN or RANKINE, this switch statement does nothing. No harm; no foul.

But the switch in Listing 8-8 is a switch expression. In the call to Math.max, the switch expression's value (either -273.15, -459.6, or 0.0) gets compared with the number field's value. So the switch expression better darn well return a value. In fact, when you write a switch expression with an enum value, you must account for each of the enum value's possibilities. You can cop out by doing something like this:

println(switch (scale) {
case CELSIUS -> "degrees Celsius";
case FAHRENHEIT -> "degrees Fahrenheit";
default -> "";
});

But the following code makes Java cry out in pain:

// Error! Error! Error!
println(switch (scale) {
case CELSIUS -> "degrees Celsius";
case FAHRENHEIT -> "degrees Fahrenheit";
});

The error message this code generates is:'switch' expression does not cover all possible input values.

Equality for all!

This chapter's “What does a temperature look like?” section tells you that every class has a toString method. If you don't write a toString method, Java creates an implicit toString method for you. It's called an inherited toString method.

The same is true of Java's equals methods. Every class has an equals method. An example in Chapter 5 shows how nice Java's inherited equals method works for String values. In fact, to find out if myName and yourName contain the same characters, you shouldn't write

if (myName == yourName) // No!

Instead, you should write

if (myName.equals(yourName)) // Yes

The String class's equals method is very useful, but the String class's equals method isn't typical. Inherited equals methods don't work well for arbitrary Java classes. Look at the main method in Listing 8-9. Figure 8-6 shows you the output when I run this main method along with the code in Listing 8-3.

LISTING 8-9 Comparing Temperatures

void main() {
var freezing1 = new Temperature(0.0, TempScale.CELSIUS);
var freezing2 = new Temperature(0.0, TempScale.CELSIUS);
println(freezing1 + " equals " + freezing2 + " ?");
println(freezing1.equals(freezing2));
println("");

var freezing3 = new Temperature(32.0, TempScale.FAHRENHEIT);
println(freezing1 + " equals " + freezing3 + " ?");
println(freezing1.equals(freezing3));
}

In Listing 8-9, the freezing1 and freezing2 variables refer to two different objects. So, with the class Listing 8-3, Java's inherited equals method says they're not equal. That's disappointing, but what else can you expect from the Temperature class in Listing 8-3? It's not a record class.

Record classes behave better than other kinds of classes. When you define Temperature to be a record class, the inherited toString method gives something like Temperature[number=2.73, scale=KELVIN]. (See Figure 8-3.) That's good! A record class's inherited toString method returns a reasonable representation of an object and its fields.

So, maybe the record class in Listing 8-7 has a nice inherited equals method. Wha' da' ya' think? Figure 8-7 shows what you get when you run the main method in Listing 8-9 along with the record class in Listing 8-7.

If you define Temperature to be a record class, Java's equals method does an “okay” job. With two 0°-Celsius objects, the equals method returns true. That's better than what you get with a class that's not a record class. But it's not the best. The inherited equals method doesn't know how to convert between temperature scales.

To solve this problem, you write your own equals method. Listing 8-10 shows you how.

LISTING 8-10 Comparing Temperatures

public record Temperature (double number, TempScale scale) {

public boolean equals(Temperature other) {
var number1 = this.toCelsius();
var number2 = other.toCelsius();
return number1 == number2;
}

public double toCelsius() {
return switch (scale) {
case CELSIUS -> number;
case FAHRENHEIT -> (number - 32) * 5.0 / 9.0;
case KELVIN -> number - 273.15;
case RANKINE -> (number - 491.67) * 5.0 / 9.0;
};
}

public String toString() {
return String.format("%5.2f\u00B0 ", number) + scale;
}
}

Combining the main method in Listing 8-9 with the Temperature class in Listing 8-10, you get the output shown in Figure 8-8.

Lo and behold! The output in Figure 8-8 is correct in both cases. It helps to write your own equals method.

So, you thought you were finished with this chapter about constructors! Well, there's more to do if you want to practice coding.

IT ISN'T WHAT IT ISN'T

Modify the code in Listing 8-2 so that none of the constructors lets you create a less-than-absolute-zero temperature. While you're at it, modify the setter methods, too.

KEEP IT SHORT AND SWEET

Change the code you wrote in this chapter's “School days” and “Flight of fancy” sections. Turn both classes into record classes.

Chapter 9

Piles of Files: Dealing with Information Overload

IN THIS CHAPTER

Using data on your hard drive

Writing code to access the hard drive

Troubleshooting input/output behavior

Consider these scenarios:

  • You’re a business owner who handles hundreds of invoices each day. You store invoice data in a file on your hard drive. You need customized code to sort and classify the invoices.
  • You’re an astronomer with data from scans of the night sky. When you’re ready to analyze a chunk of data, you load the chunk onto your computer’s hard drive.
  • You’re the author of a popular self-help book. Last year’s fad was the Self-Mirroring Method. This year’s craze is the Make Your Cake System. You can’t modify your manuscript without converting it to the publisher’s new specifications. You need software to make the task bearable.

Each situation calls for a new computer program, and each program reads from a large data file. On top of all of that, each program creates a brand-new file containing bright, shiny results.

In previous chapters, the examples get input from the keyboard and send output to a text window. That’s fine for small tasks, but you can’t have the computer prompt you for each bit of night sky data. For big problems, you need lots of data, and the best place to store the data is on a computer’s hard drive.

What It Means to Be an Employee

When you write an object-oriented program, you start by thinking about the data. You’re writing about accounts. So, what’s an account? You’re writing code to handle button clicks. So, what’s a button? You’re writing a program to send payroll checks to employees. What’s an employee?

In this chapter’s first example, an employee is someone with a name and a job title. Sure, employees have other characteristics, but for now, I stick to the basics. The code in Listing 9-1 defines what it means to be an employee.

LISTING 9-1 What Is an Employee?

public class Employee {
private String name;
private String jobTitle;

public void setName(String name) {
this.name = name;
}

public String getName() {
return name;
}

public void setJobTitle(String jobTitle) {
this.jobTitle = jobTitle;
}

public String getJobTitle() {
return jobTitle;
}

public void cutCheck(double amountPaid) {
System.out.print("Pay to the order of " + name);
System.out.print(" (");
System.out.print(jobTitle);
System.out.print(") ***$");
System.out.println(String.format("%,.2f", amountPaid));
}
}

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN I LISTEN TO OTHER PEOPLE

The curious reader may be interested in some history concerning Listing 9-1. In this book's first few editions, the Employee class listing looked like this:

public class Employee {
String name;
String jobTitle;

public void cutCheck(double amountPaid) {
System.out.print("Pay to the order of " + name);
System.out.print(" (");
System.out.print(jobTitle);
System.out.print(") ***$");
System.out.println(String.format("%,.2f", amountPaid));
}
}

The Employee class code was short and sweet. But a colleague of mine read the code and remarked that “real” Java programmers wouldn't write code this way. They would make the name and jobTitle fields private. They'd compensate for the use of private fields by adding public getter and setter methods.

At first, I paid no attention to my colleague. I insisted that each of my book's examples be as short and simple as possible. I wanted readers to see the bare-bones concepts without fuss or fanfare. But, one or two editions later, I caught the “make programs look professional” disease. I made the book's examples longer and more complicated. That's why this edition's Listing 9-1 has more moving parts than the version in this sidebar.

I confess, dear reader! I'm ambivalent about my tendency to create more elaborate examples. But I also realize that first impressions make a difference. You're entitled to start your Java journey with code that's written the “right way.” So, here and in other chapters, I let you take your pick. This sidebar's code illustrates essentially the same concepts as the code in Listing 9-1. “Each employee has a name, a job title, and a way of cutting a check.” That's the story in a nutshell.

If looking at Listing 9-1 gives you a headache, bypass Listing 9-1 and look at this sidebar's code instead. Once you've become comfortable with the notion of an Employee class, you can return to Listing 9-1. Then, and only then, should you think about private fields, public accessor methods, and all the other gems that make professional programmers so very happy.

The Employee class in Listing 9-1 has seven members. Two of these members are fairly simple: Each employee has a name field and a jobTitle field.

The other five Employee members are methods. For example, each employee has four methods to handle the values of the employee's name and job title. These methods are setName, getName, setJobTitle, and getJobTitle. I explain methods like these (getter and setter methods) in Chapter 7.

On top of all of that, each employee has a cutCheck method. The idea is that the method that writes payroll checks has to belong to one class or another. Because most of the information in the payroll check is customized for a particular employee, you may as well put the cutCheck method inside the Employee class.

The print, println, and readln methods that I use in many examples didn't become part of Java until September 2024, and then only as a preview feature. Until then, the easiest way to display text on the screen was to call the System.out.println method. (See Listing 9-1.)

Putting your class to good use

The Employee class in Listing 9-1 has no main method, so there's no starting point for executing code. To fix this deficiency, the programmer writes a separate program with a main method and uses that program to create Employee instances. Listing 9-2 shows a class with a main method — one that puts the code in Listing 9-1 to the test.

LISTING 9-2 The Check Is in the Mail

import java.util.Scanner;

public class PayOneEmployee {

public static void main(String[] args) {
var keyboard = new Scanner(System.in);

var name = keyboard.nextLine();
var jobTitle = keyboard.next();

var anEmployee = new Employee();
anEmployee.setName(name);
anEmployee.setJobTitle(jobTitle);

var pay = keyboard.nextDouble();

anEmployee.cutCheck(pay);
}
}

For a run of the code in Listing 9-1, see Figure 9-1.

SIMPLIFY, SIMPLIFY!

No matter what you do, there's always a more difficult way of doing it.

Listing 9-2 uses the traditional way of writing main methods. In the old style, every method must be inside an explicit class, every main method must be public and static, every main method must have a String[] args parameter, and so on, and so forth. If you use the newer features (available as preview features in Java 23), you get this simplified code:

void main() {
var keyboard = new Scanner(System.in);

var name = keyboard.nextLine();
var jobTitle = keyboard.next();

var anEmployee = new Employee();
anEmployee.setName(name);
anEmployee.setJobTitle(jobTitle);

var pay = keyboard.nextDouble();

anEmployee.cutCheck(pay);
}

If you're willing to change the way a user interacts with the program, you can make it even simpler:

void main() {
var name = readln("Name? ");
var jobTitle = readln("Job title? ");

var anEmployee = new Employee();
anEmployee.setName(name);
anEmployee.setJobTitle(jobTitle);

var pay = Double.parseDouble(readln("Pay? "));

anEmployee.cutCheck(pay);
}

Both of these main methods play nicely with Listing 9-1.

Back in Listing 9-1, notice the comma inside the %,.2f placeholder. The comma tells the program to use grouping separators. That's why, in Figure 9-1, you see 5,000.00 instead of 5000.00. If you run the same program with the statement

java.util.Locale.setDefault(new java.util.Locale("kl", "GL"));

you get the Greenland Kalaallisut version of five thousand, which is 5.000,00.

She reads keystrokes from the keyboard

In Listing 9-2, the code

import java.util.Scanner;

var keyboard = new Scanner(System.in);

int name = keyboard.nextLine();

performs almost the same function as this single statement:

var name = IO.readln(""); // or, in Java 24 and beyond, IO.readln();

The code gets whatever text the user types on a single line on the computer's keyboard. In addition, the code stores this text in the program's name variable. Here are some facts about this use of Java's Scanner class:

  • Typically (on a desktop or laptop computer), the name System.in stands for the keyboard.

    To get characters from someplace other than the keyboard, you can type something other than System.in inside the parentheses.

    What else can you put inside the new Scanner(…) parentheses? For some ideas, see this chapter's later section “Working with Disk Files.”

    In Listing 9-2, I make the arbitrary decision to give one of my variables the name keyboard. The name keyboard reminds you, the reader, that this variable refers to a bunch of plastic buttons in front of your computer. Naming something keyboard doesn't tell Java anything about plastic buttons or about user input. On the other hand, the name System.in always tells Java about those plastic buttons. The code var keyboard = new Scanner(System.in) in Listing 9-2 connects the name keyboard with the plastic buttons that we all know and love.

  • Java's Scannerclass has several different nextSomethingOrOthermethods.

    Here are some examples:

    • The nextDouble method reads a double value (a number containing a decimal point). Listing 9-2 calls nextDouble to get a payment amount.

      The representation of decimal points varies from one country to another. For details (and some interesting trivia), see this chapter's later sidebar “Where on Earth do you live?”

    • The nextInt method reads an int value (a whole number of some kind).

    • The next method reads a single word — a bunch of text up to, but not including, some white space. In Figure 9-1, the call keyboard.next() gets the word CEO and nothing else.

      By the way, the term white space means a blank space, a tab character, the end of a line, and several other oddities.

    • The nextLine method gets everything up to the end of a line. In Figure 9-1, a call to nextLine scoops up everything on one line of input (both words Barry and Burd).

      Some surprising things happen when you combine nextLine with other Scanner methods. For details, see this chapter's later section “Reading a line at a time.”

  • Whenever you use Java's Scanner, you should call the close method after your last nextWhatever call.

    In Listing 9-2, the main method's last statement is

    keyboard.close();

    This statement does some housekeeping to disconnect the Java program from the computer keyboard. (The amount of required housekeeping is more than you might think!) If I omit this statement from Listing 9-2, nothing terrible happens. Java usually cleans up after itself very nicely. But using close() to explicitly detach from the keyboard is good practice, and some IDEs display warnings if you omit the keyboard.close() statement. In this book's example, I always remember to close my Scanner variables.

    In Chapter 14, I show you a more reliable way to incorporate the keyboard.close() statement in your Java program.

The listings in previous chapters use Java's readln method to get input from the keyboard. So, why not use readln here in Listing 9-2? As of September 2024, with the release of Java 23, the newly-created readln method works only with keyboard input. If you want to get data from a disk file, you can't use the readln method. And no one wants to go through life without reading from a disk file. Relying exclusively on keyboard input is too confining. If you have several employees, you store employee information on a disk.

Java has many classes and methods for reading input of various kinds. The Scanner class from Listing 9-2 dates back to the release of Java 5.0 in 2004. A more versatile input package, java.nio, was born in 2002 as part of Java 1.4. And the venerable InputStreamReader/BufferedReader classes came with Java 1.0 in 1996.

In any programming language, with input of any kind, there's a lot going on under the hood. Your program sets up a connection between the code and the storage device, prepares for possible trouble reading from the device, does the reading, converts the characters it reads into the type of value that you want and, finally, breaks your connection with the storage device. And the underlying operating system does even more work. It's a big mess.

Java's Scanner class doesn't offer all the options you get with the old Java 1.0 classes or with java.nio. In exchange for its lack of versatility, the Scanner class makes disk input fairly simple. Even so, disk input with Scanner can confuse novice programmers. So, the next section translates Listing 9-2 into a program that reads from a disk file using the Scanner class.

There are always interesting things for you to try:

GO, SCANNER, GO

Write a program that reads two double values separated by an arithmetic operator sign and uses a switch structure to do the arithmetic. For example, if the user types 2.0 * 5.1, the program outputs 10.2.

LOCALE, LOCALE, LOCALE

A PlaceToLive has an address, a number of bedrooms, and an area (in square feet or square meters). Write the PlaceToLive class's code. Write code for a main method that creates a few PlaceToLive instances by assigning values to their address, numberOfBedrooms, and area fields. The main method also reads (from the keyboard) the cost of living in each place. For each place, your code displays the cost per square foot (or square meter) and the cost per bedroom.

Working with Disk Files

Your company is growing. In Listing 9-3, you had only one employee. In the next listing, you have three!

LISTING 9-3 Writing Payroll Checks

import java.io.File; // These imports are optional for
import java.io.IOException; // a simple source file
import java.util.Scanner; // (like this file, for example).

void main() throws IOException {
var diskScanner = new Scanner(new File("EmployeeInfo.txt"));

for (int empNum = 1; empNum <= 3; empNum++) {
var anEmployee = new Employee();

anEmployee.setName(diskScanner.nextLine());
anEmployee.setJobTitle(diskScanner.nextLine());
anEmployee.cutCheck(diskScanner.nextDouble());
diskScanner.nextLine();
}

diskScanner.close();
}

The for loop in Listing 9-3 performs three iterations. Here's how the variable name anEmployee is reused and recycled during those iterations:

  • During the first iteration, the statement anEmployee = new Employee() makes anEmployee refer to a new object.
  • During the second iteration, the computer executes the same statement again. This second execution creates a new incarnation of the anEmployee variable that refers to a brand-new object.
  • During the third iteration, all the same stuff happens again. A new anEmployee variable ends up referring to a third object.

The whole story is pictured in Figure 9-2.

To run the code in Listing 9-3, your hard drive must contain a file named EmployeeInfo.txt. Fortunately, the stuff that you download from this book's website (http://javafordummies.allmycode.com) comes with an EmployeeInfo.txt file. Just copy the EmployeeInfo.txt file to a place where Listing 9-3 can find it.

For help deciding where Listing 9-3 can find the file, see this chapter's “Where's your file?” section.

Figure 9-3 shows the EmployeeInfo.txt file you get when you visit this book's website and download the book's code.

You can create your own EmployeeInfo.txt file with Windows Notepad or TextEdit on a Mac. (If you use TextEdit, be sure to choose Settings ⇒   Format ⇒   Plain Text.) When you type the characters in Figure 9-3, you must finish up by typing 10000.00 and then pressing Enter. (Look again at Figure 9-3 and notice how the cursor is at the start of a brand-new line.) If you forget to finish by pressing Enter, the code in Listing 9-3 will crash when you try to run it.

And remember: Grouping separators vary from one country to another. The file shown in Figure 9-3 works on a computer configured in the United States where 5000.00 means “five thousand.” But the file doesn't work on a computer that's configured in what I call a “comma country” — a country where 5000,00 means “five thousand.” If you live in a comma country, be sure to read this chapter's nearby sidebar “Where on Earth do you live?”

Figure 9-4 shows the output when you run Listing 9-3 using EmployeeInfo.txt file in Figure 9-3.

WHERE ON EARTH DO YOU LIVE?

Grouping separators vary from one country to another. In the United States, 10.5 (with a period) represents ten-and-a-half, but in France, 10,5 (with a comma) represents ten-and-a-half. In India, you group digits in sets of two and three. For example, you write 1,23,45,67,890.55. Your computer's operating system stores information about the country you live in, and Java reads that information to decide how numbers should look.

This makes a big difference when you try to read double values using Java's Scanner class. To see what I mean, have a serious look at this slightly edited JShell session:

jshell> import java.util.Scanner
jshell> import java.util.Scanner; import java.util.Locale

jshell> var keyboard = new Scanner(System.in)
keyboard ==> java.util.Scanner

jshell> keyboard.nextDouble()
1000
$4 ==> 1000.0

jshell> Locale.setDefault(Locale.FRANCE); keyboard = new Scanner(System.in)
keyboard ==> java.util.Scanner

jshell> keyboard.nextDouble()
1000,00
$7 ==> 1000.0

jshell> keyboard.nextDouble()
1000.00
| Exception java.util.InputMismatchException
| at Scanner.throwFor (Scanner.java:964)
| at Scanner.next (Scanner.java:1619)
| at Scanner.nextDouble (Scanner.java:2590)

I conducted this session on a computer in the United States. The country of origin is relevant because, in response to the first keyboard.nextDouble() call, I type 1000.00 (with a period before the last two zeros) and Java accepts this as meaning “one thousand.”

But then, in the JShell session, I call Locale.setDefault(Locale.FRANCE), which tells Java to behave as if my computer is in France. When I create another Scanner instance and call keyboard.nextDouble() again, Java accepts 1000,00 (with a comma before the last two zeros) as an expression meaning mille (French for “one thousand”). What's more, Java no longer accepts the period in 1000.00. When I type 1000.00 (with a period), I get an InputMismatchException.

By default, Java wants you to input double numbers the way you normally type them in your country. If you type numbers according to another country's convention, you get an InputMismatchException. So, when you run the code in Listing 9-3, the numbers in your EmployeeInfo.txt file must use your country's format.

This brings me to the running of the code in Listing 9-3. The EmployeeInfo.txt file that you download from this book's website starts with the following three lines:

Barry Burd
CEO
5000.00

That last number 5000.00 has a period in it, so if your country prefers a comma in place of my United States period, you get an InputMismatchException. In response to this, you have two choices:

  • In the downloaded EmployeeInfo.txt file, change the periods to commas.
  • In the code of Listing 9-3, add the statement Locale.setDefault(Locale.US) before the diskScanner declaration.

And finally, if you want your output to look like your own country's numbers, you can do it with Java's String class. Add something like this to your code:

println(String.format(java.util.Locale.FRANCE, "%,.2f", 1000.00));

For all the details, see the API (Application Programming Interface) documentation for Java's Formatter class (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Formatter.html) and Locale class (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Locale.html).

Cutting a check

In previous chapters, programs read characters from the computer's keyboard. But the code in Listing 9-3 reads characters from a specific file. The file (named EmployeeInfo.txt) lives on your computer's hard drive.

This EmployeeInfo.txt file is like a word processing document. The file can contain letters, digits, and other characters. But unlike a word processing document, the EmployeeInfo.txt file contains no formatting — no italics, no bold, no font sizes, nothing of that kind.

The EmployeeInfo.txt file contains only ordinary characters — the kinds of keystrokes that you type while you play a guessing game from Chapters 5 and 6. Of course, getting guesses from a user's keyboard and reading employee data from a disk file aren't exactly the same. In a guessing game, the program displays prompts, such as Pick a number from 1 to 10. The game program conducts a back-and-forth dialogue with the person sitting at the keyboard. In contrast, Listing 9-3 has no dialogue. This DoPayroll program reads characters from a hard drive and doesn't prompt or interact with anyone.

Repeat after me

In almost any computer programming language, reading data from a file can be tricky. You add extra lines of code to tell the computer what to do. Sometimes you can copy and paste these lines from other people's code. For example, you can follow this pattern (extracted from Listing 9-3):

/*
* The pattern in Listing 9-3
*/
import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.Scanner;

void main() throws IOException {

var scannerName = new Scanner(new File("SomeFileName"));

//Some code goes here

scannerName.nextInt();
scannerName.nextDouble();
scannerName.next();
scannerName.nextLine();
//Some code goes here

scannerName.close();
}

You want to read data from a file. You start by imagining that you're reading from the keyboard. Put the usual Scanner and next codes into your program. Then add some extra items from the Listing 9-3 pattern:

  • Add three new import declarations: one for java.io.File, another for java.io.IOException, and a third for java.util.Scanner. (With a file that has an implicitly declared class, like the file in Listing 9-3, these imports are optional.)
  • Type throws IOException in your method's header.
  • Type new File(" ") in your call to new Scanner.
  • Take a file that's already on your hard drive. Type that filename inside the quotation marks.
  • Take the word that you use for the name of your scanner. Reuse that word in calls to next, nextInt, nextDouble, and so on.
