  • Take the word that you use for the name of your scanner. Reuse that word in a call to close.

Occasionally, copying and pasting code can get you into trouble. Maybe you're writing a program that doesn't fit the simple Listing 9-3 pattern. You need to tweak the pattern a bit. But to tweak the pattern, you need to understand some of the ideas behind the pattern.

That’s how the next section comes to your rescue. It covers some of these ideas.

Reading from a file

To read characters from a file, you can use the Scanner class and methods like nextLine and nextDouble. But in addition to these goodies, you have a few extra hurdles to jump. Here's a list:

  • You need a new Fileobject. To be more precise, you need a new instance of the API's File class. You get this new instance with code like

    new File("EmployeeInfo.txt")

    The stuff in quotation marks is the name of a file — a file on your computer’s hard drive. The file contains characters like those shown previously in Figure 9-3.

    At this point, the terminology makes mountains out of molehills. Sure, I use the phrases new File object and new File instance, but all you’re doing is making new File("EmployeeInfo.txt") stand for a file on your hard drive. After you shove new File("EmployeeInfo.txt") into new Scanner,

    var diskScanner = new Scanner(new File("EmployeeInfo.txt"));

    you can forget all about the new File business. From that point on in the code, diskScanner stands for the EmployeeInfo.txt file on your computer's hard drive. (The name diskScanner stands for a file on your hard drive just as, in previous examples, the name keyboard stands for those buttons you press day in and day out.)

    Creating a new File object in Listing 9-3 is like creating a new Employee object later in the same listing. It's also like creating a new Account object in the examples of Chapter 7. The only difference is that the Employee and Account classes are defined in this book's examples. The File class is defined in Java's API.

    When you connect to a disk file with new Scanner, don't forget the new File part. If you write new Scanner("EmployeeInfo.txt") without new File, Java's compiler doesn't mind. (You don't get any warnings or error messages before you run the code.) But when you run the code, you don't get anything like the results that you expect to get.

  • You need a throws IOExceptionclause. Lots of things can go wrong when your program connects to EmployeeInfo.txt. For one thing, your hard drive may not have a file named EmployeeInfo.txt. For another, the file EmployeeInfo.txt may be in the wrong directory. To brace for this kind of calamity, the Java programming language takes certain precautions. The language insists that when a disk file is involved, you acknowledge the possible dangers of calling new Scanner.

    You can acknowledge the hazards in several possible ways, but the simplest way is to use a throws clause. In Listing 9-3, the main method's header ends with the words throws IOException. By adding these two words, you appease the Java compiler. It's as if you’re saying “I know that calling new Scanner can lead to problems. You don’t have to remind me.” And, sure enough, adding throws IOException to your main method keeps Java from complaining. (Without this throws clause, you get an unhandled exception error message.)

    For the full story on Java exceptions, read Chapter 14. In the meantime, add throws IOException to the header of any method that calls new Scanner(new File( … )).

Where's your file?

If Java can't find an EmployeeInfo.txt file, the whole project doesn't run properly. Instead, you get a FileNotFoundException.

In general, when you get a FileNotFoundException, some file that your program needs isn't available to it. This is an easy mistake to make. It can be frustrating because, to you, a file such as EmployeeInfo.txt may look like it's available to your program. But remember: Computers are stupid. If you make a tiny mistake, the computer can’t read between the lines for you. If the filename is spelled incorrectly, the computer chokes when it tries to run your code.

Sometimes you know darn well that an EmployeeInfo.txt (or whatever.xyz) file exists on your hard drive. But when you run your program, you still get a mean-looking FileNotFoundException. When this happens, the file may be in the wrong directory on your hard drive. (Of course, it depends on your point of view. Maybe the file is in the right directory but your Java program is looking for the file in the wrong directory.) To diagnose this problem, add the following code to Listing 9-3:

var employeeInfo = new File("EmployeeInfo.txt");
System.out.println("Looking for " + employeeInfo.getCanonicalPath());

When you run the code, Java tells you where, on your hard drive, the EmployeeInfo.txt file should be.

You can decide where to put your file

With code like new File("EmployeeInfo.txt"), your IDE decides where to look for a file named EmployeeInfo.txt. But you can override this behavior by naming a file's exact location in your Java code. Code like new File("C:\\Users\\bburd\\Documents\\EmployeeInfo.txt") on Windows or File("/Users/bburd/Documents/EmployeeInfo.txt") on a Mac looks really ugly, but it works.

In the preceding paragraph, did you notice the double backslashes in"C: \\Users\\bburd\\Documents …"? If you're a Windows user, you'd be tempted to write C:\Users\bburd\Documents … with single backslashes. But in Java, the single backslash has its own, special meaning. (For example, print("\n\nBoo!") means, “Skip two lines and then print Boo!.”) So, in Java, to indicate a backslash inside a quoted string, you use a double backslash instead.

Reading a line at a time

Listings 9-2 and 9-3 illustrate some useful tricks for reading data. In particular, every scanner that you create has a nextLine method. (You might not use this nextLine method, but the method is available nonetheless.) When you call a scanner's nextLine method, the method grabs everything up to the end of the current line of text.

In the previous paragraph, notice my careful choice of words: nextLine reads everything “up to the end of the current line.” Unfortunately, what it means to read up to the end of the current line isn't always what you think it means. Intermingling nextInt, nextDouble, and nextLine calls can be messy. You have to watch what you're doing and check your program's output carefully.

To understand all of this, you need to be painfully aware of a data file’s line breaks. Think of a line break as an extra character, stuck between one line of text and the next. Then imagine that calling nextLine means to read everything up to and including the next line break.

Figure 9-5 contains an annotated version of the first several lines in Figure 9-3. Notice what you do to read 5000.00 followed by Harriet Ritter:

  • You call nextDouble to get 5000.00 and then,
  • You call nextLine, thinking that you'll get Harriet Ritter from the call. But, instead, you get the line break after 5000.00.

So, after reading the number 5000.00, you need two calls to nextLine in order to scoop up the name Harriet Ritter. The mistake that I usually make is to forget the first of those two calls.

Look again at the file in Figure 9-3. For this section's code to work correctly, you must have a line break after the last 10000.00. If you don't, a final call to nextLine makes your program crash and burn. The error message reads NoSuchElementException: No line found.

I'm always surprised by the number of quirks that I find in each programming language's scanning methods. For example, the first nextLine that reads from the file in Figure 9-3 devours Barry Burd[LineBreak] from the file. But that nextLine call delivers Barry Burd (with no line break) to the running code. So nextLine looks for a line break, and then nextLine loses the line break. Yes, this is a subtle point. And no, this subtle point hardly ever causes problems for anyone.

If this business about nextDouble and nextLine confuses you, please don't put the blame on Java. Mixing input calls is delicate work in any computer programming language. And the truly nasty thing is that each programming language approaches the problem a little differently. What you find out about nextLine in Java helps you understand the issues when you get to know C++ or Visual Basic, but it doesn't tell you all the details. Each language’s details are unique to that language. (Yes, it’s a big pain. But because all computer programmers become rich and famous, the pain eventually pays off.)

Clean up after yourself

To the average computer user, a keyboard doesn't feel anything like a file stored on a computer's hard drive. But disk files and keyboard input have a lot in common. In fact, a basic principle of computer operating systems dictates that any differences between two kinds of input be, for the programmer, as blurry as possible. As a Java programmer, you should treat disk files and keyboard input almost the same way. That's why Listing 9-3 contains a diskScanner.close() call.

When you run a Java program, you normally execute the main method's statements, starting with the first statement in the method body and ending with the last statement in the method body. You take detours along the way, skipping past else parts and diving into method bodies, but basically you finish executing statements at the end of the main method. That's why, in Listing 9-3, the call to close is at the end of the main method's body. When you run the code in Listing 9-3, the last thing you do is disconnect from the disk file. And, fortunately, that disconnection takes place after you've executed all the nextLine and nextDouble calls.

ON THE RECORD

Previously in this chapter, you create instances of your own PlaceToLive class and display information about those instances. Modify the text-based version of your code so that it gets each instance's characteristics (address, number of bedrooms, and area) from a disk file.

Chapter 10

Saving Time and Money: Reusing Existing Code

IN THIS CHAPTER

Adding new life to old code

Tweaking your code

Making changes without spending a fortune

reuse /ree-YOOSS/ noun The act of using something for the nth time, where n is greater than 1. Example: “Reuse of the material in Java For Dummies, 9th Edition, is strictly prohibited.”

Reuse is good but, in many situations, reuse is a rarity. For example, in the United States, the Department of Agriculture estimates that 30 to 40 percent of the nation's food goes to waste. And, according to one source, only 9 percent of the world's plastics are recycled.

Information goes to waste too. When I revised this chapter for the eighth edition, I decided not to reuse the seventh edition's chapter introduction. (That introduction's made-up story isn't amusing in the least.) In desperation, I looked at some of my other books to find an introduction that I could reuse for this chapter. No luck! I came up empty-handed.

I can't even reuse paragraphs to explain common concepts. My description of Java classes from another book wouldn't work well in this book. I've even experienced times when I had to scrap sections in several chapters because of a small update in Chapter 3.

No doubt about it! Reuse is a precious commodity, and it's in very short supply. Wouldn’t it be nice if every piece of software did just what you wanted it to do? In an ideal world, you could buy a program, make it work right away, plug it seamlessly into new situations, and update it easily whenever your needs change. Unfortunately, software of this kind doesn’t exist. (Nothing of this kind exists.) The truth is that no matter what you want to do, you can find software that does some of it, but not all of it.

This is one of the reasons why object-oriented programming has been successful. For years, companies were buying prewritten code, only to discover that the code didn’t do what they wanted it to do. So, what did the companies do about it? They started messing with the code. Their programmers dug deep into the program files, changed variable names, moved subprograms around, reworked formulas, and generally made the code worse. The reality was that if a program didn’t already do what you wanted it to do (even if it did something ever so close to what you wanted), you could never improve the situation by mucking around inside the code. The best option was always to chuck the whole program (expensive as that was) and start all over again. What a sad state of affairs!

With object-oriented programming, a big change has come about. At its heart, an object-oriented program is made to be modified. With correctly written software, you can take advantage of features that are already built-in, add new features of your own, and override features that don’t suit your needs. And the best part is that the changes you make are clean — no clawing and digging into other people’s brittle program code. Instead, you make nice, orderly additions and modifications without touching the existing code’s internal logic. It’s the ideal solution.

Defining Subclasses (What It Means to Be a Full-Time or Part-Time Employee)

This time last year, your company paid $10 million for a piece of software. (Too bad! You didn't know you could find that software in Chapter 9 of Java For Dummies, 9th Edition.)

The software came in the form of an Employee.class file. People at Burd Brain Consulting (the company that created the software) didn't want you to know about the innards of the software. (They didn't want you to steal their ideas.) So, you don't have the Java program file that the software came from. In other words, you don’t have the Employee.java file in Listing 9-1 (over in Chapter 9) and Listing 10-1.

LISTING 10-1 What Is an Employee?

public class Employee {
private String name;
private String jobTitle;

public void setName(String name) {
this.name = name;
}

public String getName() {
return name;
}

public void setJobTitle(String jobTitle) {
this.jobTitle = jobTitle;
}

public String getJobTitle() {
return jobTitle;
}

public void cutCheck(double amountPaid) {
System.out.print("Pay to the order of " + name);
System.out.print(" (");
System.out.print(jobTitle);
System.out.print(") ***$");
System.out.println(String.format("%,.2f", amountPaid));
}
}

You can run the bytecode in the Employee.class file. You can also read the documentation in a web page named Employee.html. But you can't see the statements inside the Employee.java program, and you can't change any of the program’s code.

Chapter 2 describes the difference between filenames ending with .java and those ending with .class. To write code that uses the Employee class, you don't need the Employee.java file on your hard drive. All you need is the file Employee.class.

Since this time last year, your company has grown. Unlike in the old days, your company now has two kinds of employees: full-time and part-time. Each full-time employee is on a fixed, weekly salary. (If the employee works nights and weekends, then in return for this monumental effort, the employee receives a hearty handshake.) In contrast, each part-time employee works for an hourly wage. Your company deducts an amount from each full-time employee's paycheck to pay for the company’s benefits package. Part-time employees, however, don’t get benefits.

The question is whether the software that your company bought last year can keep up with the company’s growth. You invested in a helpful program to handle employees and their payroll, but the program doesn’t differentiate between your full-time and part-time employees. You have several options:

  • Call your next-door neighbor, whose 12-year-old child knows more about computer programming than anyone in your company. Get this uppity little brat to take the employee software apart, rewrite it, and hand it back to you with all the changes and additions your company requires.

    On second thought, you can’t do that. No matter how smart that kid is, the complexities of the employee software will probably confuse the kid. By the time you get the software back, it’ll be filled with bugs and inconsistencies. Besides, you don’t even have the Employee.java file to hand to the kid. All you have is the Employee.class file, which is bytecode. And bytecode can't be read or modified with a text editor. (See Chapter 2.) Besides, your kid just beat up the neighbor's kid. You don’t want to give your neighbor the satisfaction of seeing you beg for the whiz kid’s help.

  • Scrap the $10 million employee software. Persuade someone in your company to rewrite the software from scratch.

    In other words, say goodbye to your time and money.

  • Write a new front end for the employee software. That is, build a piece of code that does some preliminary processing on full-time employees and then hands the preliminary results to your $10 million software. Do the same for part-time employees.

    This idea could be decent or spell disaster. Are you sure that the existing employee software has convenient hooks in it? (That is, does the employee software contain entry points that allow your front-end software to easily send preliminary data to the expensive employee software?) Remember: This plan treats the existing software as one big, monolithic lump, which can become cumbersome. Dividing the labor between your front-end code and the existing employee program is difficult. And, if you add layer upon layer to existing black box code, you’ll probably end up with a fairly inefficient system.

  • Call Burd Brain Consulting, the company that sold you the employee software. Tell Dr. Burd that you want the next version of his software to differentiate between full-time and part-time employees.

    “No problem,” says Dr. Burd. “It’ll be ready by the start of the next fiscal quarter.” That evening, Dr. Burd makes a discreet phone call to his next-door neighbor… .

  • Create two new Java classes named FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee. Have each new class extend the existing functionality of the expensive Employee class, but have each new class define its own, specialized functionality for certain kinds of employees.

    Way to go! Figure 10-1 shows the structure that you want to create.

Creating a subclass

Listing 10-1 defines an Employee class. You may not have access to the Employee.java file, but if you have the compiled Employee.class file and some documentation about the code, you can extend the definition of an Employee to create new, more specialized classes. So, in Listing 10-2, I define a new class: a FullTimeEmployee class.

LISTING 10-2 What Is a FullTimeEmployee?

public class FullTimeEmployee extends Employee {
private double weeklySalary;
private double benefitDeduction;

public void setWeeklySalary(double weeklySalary) {
this.weeklySalary = weeklySalary;
}

public double getWeeklySalary() {
return weeklySalary;
}

public void setBenefitDeduction(double benefitDeduction) {
this.benefitDeduction = benefitDeduction;
}

public double getBenefitDeduction() {
return benefitDeduction;
}

public double findPaymentAmount() {
return weeklySalary - benefitDeduction;
}
}

Looking at Listing 10-2, you can see that each instance of the FullTimeEmployee class has two fields: weeklySalary and benefitDeduction. But are those the only fields that each FullTimeEmployee instance has? No, they're not. The first line of Listing 10-2 says that the FullTimeEmployee class extends the existing Employee class. This means that in addition to having a weeklySalary and a benefitDeduction, each FullTimeEmployee instance has two other fields: name and jobTitle. These two fields come from the definition of the Employee class, which you can find in Listing 10-1.

In Listing 10-2, the magic word is extends. When one class extends an existing class, the extending class implicitly inherits functionality that's defined in the existing class. So, the FullTimeEmployee class inherits the name and jobTitle fields. The FullTimeEmployee class also inherits all the methods that are declared in the Employee class: setName, getName, setJobTitle, getJobTitle, and cutCheck.

The FullTimeEmployee class is a subclass of the Employee class. That means the Employee class is the superclass of the FullTimeEmployee class. You can also talk in terms of blood relatives: The FullTimeEmployee class is the child of the Employee class, and the Employee class is the parent of the FullTimeEmployee class.

IGNORANCE IS BLISS

I'm a big believer in the value of ignoring details. When I look at Listing 10-2, I ignore most of the text. I see only a few words surrounded by some curly braces.

public class FullTimeEmployee extends Employee {
double weeklySalary;
double benefitDeduction;
double findPaymentAmount() {
return weeklySalary - benefitDeduction;
}
}

I see a class with two fields and a findPaymentAmount method. I also see the words extends Employee, and I say to myself “The words extends Employee don't appear in any of the previous chapters. So, the rest of this chapter should be about words like extends Employee.” And, indeed, the rest of this chapter is about extending classes.

This sidebar's code is much shorter than the code in Listing 10-2. But that's because this sidebar's code doesn't do things exactly the same way as the code in Listing 10-2. In particular, the code in Listing 10-2 has private fields with accessor methods. So, later in this chapter (Listing 10-5, in fact), you see the following lines:

var ftEmployee = new FullTimeEmployee();
ftEmployee.setWeeklySalary(5000.00);

The second of these lines calls the setWeeklySalary method in Listing 10-2. That's all well and good, but if you use this sidebar's simpler FullTimeEmployee class, you write the following code instead:

var ftEmployee = new FullTimeEmployee();
ftEmployee.weeklySalary = 5000.00;

Instead of setWeeklySalary(5000.00), you write weeklySalary = 5000.00. The first time you see these two code snippets, you may have trouble distinguishing one from the other. But when you've had practice writing several Java programs, you stop fretting about parentheses and equal signs. You simply remember that a FullTimeEmployee has a weekly salary, a benefit deduction, and can find its own payment amount. Also, in some way, shape, or form, a full-time employee extends Employee.

Several names from Listing 10-1 are implicitly defined in Listing 10-2. It's almost (but not quite) as if the FullTimeEmployee class were defined by the code in Listing 10-3.

LISTING 10-3 Fake (but Informative) Code

public class FullTimeEmployee {
private String name;
private String jobTitle;
private double weeklySalary;
private double benefitDeduction;

public void setName(String name) {
this.name = name;
}

public String getName() {
return name;
}

public void setJobTitle(String jobTitle) {
this.jobTitle = jobTitle;
}

public String getJobTitle() {
return jobTitle;
}

public void setWeeklySalary(double weeklySalary) {
this.weeklySalary = weeklySalary;
}

public double getWeeklySalary() {
return weeklySalary;
}

public void setBenefitDeduction(double benefitDeduction) {
this.benefitDeduction = benefitDeduction;
}

public double getBenefitDeduction() {
return benefitDeduction;
}

public double findPaymentAmount() {
return weeklySalary - benefitDeduction;
}

public void cutCheck(double amountPaid) {
System.out.print("Pay to the order of " + name);
System.out.print(" (");
System.out.print(jobTitle);
System.out.print(") ***$");
System.out.println(String.format("%,.2f", amountPaid));
}
}

Why does the title for Listing 10-3 call that code “fake”? (Should the code feel insulted?) Well, the main difference between Listing 10-3 and the inheritance situation in Listings 10-1 and 10-2 is this: A child class can't directly reference the private fields of its parent class. To do anything with the parent class’s private fields, the child class has to call the parent class’s getter and setter methods. Back in Listing 10-2, calling setName("Rufus") would be legal, but the code name="Rufus" wouldn't be. If you believe everything you read in Listing 10-3, you'd think that code in the FullTimeEmployee class can do name="Rufus". Well, it can't. (My, what a subtle point this is!)

Creating subclasses is habit-forming

After you're accustomed to extending classes, you can get extend-happy. If you created a FullTimeEmployee class, you might as well create a PartTimeEmployee class, as shown in Listing 10-4.

LISTING 10-4 What Is a PartTimeEmployee?

public class PartTimeEmployee extends Employee {
private double hourlyRate;

public void setHourlyRate(double hourlyRate) {
this.hourlyRate = hourlyRate;
}

public double getHourlyRate() {
return hourlyRate;
}

public double findPaymentAmount(int hours) {
return hourlyRate * hours;
}
}

Unlike the FullTimeEmployee class, PartTimeEmployee has no salary or deduction. Instead, PartTimeEmployee has an hourlyRate field. (Adding an hoursWorked field would also be a possibility. I chose not to do this, figuring that the number of hours a part-time employee works may change from week to week.)

Using Subclasses

The preceding section tells a story about creating subclasses. It's a good story, but it's incomplete. Creating subclasses is fine, but you gain nothing from these subclasses unless you write code to use them.

Listing 10-5 contains the simplest possible example of a program that uses the subclasses FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee. (For a look at some more interesting examples, visit this book's website).

LISTING 10-5 Putting Subclasses to Good Use

void main() {

var ftEmployee = new FullTimeEmployee();

ftEmployee.setName("Barry Burd");
ftEmployee.setJobTitle("CEO");
ftEmployee.setWeeklySalary(5000.00);
ftEmployee.setBenefitDeduction(500.00);
ftEmployee.cutCheck(ftEmployee.findPaymentAmount());
println("");

var ptEmployee = new PartTimeEmployee();

ptEmployee.setName("Steve Surace");
ptEmployee.setJobTitle("Driver");
ptEmployee.setHourlyRate(7.53);
ptEmployee.cutCheck(ptEmployee.findPaymentAmount(10));
}

Figure 10-2 shows the output of the code in Listing 10-5.

To understand Listing 10-5, you need to keep an eye on three classes: Employee, FullTimeEmployee, and PartTimeEmployee. (For a look at the code that defines these classes, see Listings 10-1, 10-2, and 10-4.)

The first half of Listing 10-5 deals with a full-time employee. Notice the methods that are available for use with the ftEmployee variable. You can call ftEmployee.setWeeklySalary because ftEmployee has type FullTimeEmployee. You can also call ftEmployee.setName because the FullTimeEmployee class extends the Employee class.

Because cutCheck is declared in the Employee class, you can call ftEmployee.cutCheck. But you can also call ftEmployee.findPaymentAmount because a findPaymentAmount method is in the FullTimeEmployee class.

Subclasses embody what computer scientists call the is a relationship. Every FullTimeEmployee instance is anEmployee instance too. To make sure I'm not lying to you, run this code:

void main() {
var ftEmployee = new FullTimeEmployee();
println(ftEmployee instanceof FullTimeEmployee);
println(ftEmployee instanceof Employee);
}

The output from both println calls is the word true.

Making types match

Look again at the first half of Listing 10-5. Take special notice of the statement that cuts a check for ftEmployee. The statement forms a nice, long chain of values and their types. You can see this by reading the statement from the inside out:

  • Method ftEmployee.findPaymentAmount is called with an empty parameter list. (Refer to Listing 10-5.) That's good because a full-time employee's findPaymentAmount method takes no parameters. (Refer to Listing 10-2.)
  • The findPaymentAmount method returns a value of type double. (Again, refer to Listing 10-2.)
  • The double value that ftEmployee.findPaymentAmount returns is passed to method ftEmployee.cutCheck. (Refer to Listing 10-5.) That's good because the Employee class's cutCheck method takes one parameter of type double. (Refer to Listing 10-1.)

For a fanciful graphical illustration of this type-matching business, see Figure 10-3.

Always feed a method the value types that it wants in its parameter list.

The second half of the story

In the second half of Listing 10-5, the code creates an object of type PartTimeEmployee. A variable of type PartTimeEmployee can do some of the same things a FullTimeEmployee variable can do. But the PartTimeEmployee class doesn't have the setWeeklySalary and setBenefitDeduction methods. Instead, the PartTimeEmployee class has the setHourlyRate method. (See Listing 10-4.) So, in Listing 10-5 the next-to-last line is a call to the setHourlyRate method.

The last line of Listing 10-5 is by far the most interesting. On that line, the code hands the number 10 (the number of hours worked) to the findPaymentAmount method. Compare this with the earlier call to findPaymentAmount — the call for the full-time employee in the first half of Listing 10-5. Between the two subclasses, FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee, are two different findPaymentAmount methods. The two methods have two different kinds of parameter lists:

  • The FullTimeEmployee class's findPaymentAmount method takes no parameters (refer to Listing 10-2).
  • The PartTimeEmployee class's findPaymentAmount method takes one int parameter (refer to Listing 10-4).

This is par for the course. Finding the payment amount for a part-time employee isn't the same as finding the payment amount for a full-time employee. A part-time employee's pay changes each week, depending on the number of hours the employee works in a week. The full-time employee’s pay stays the same each week. So, the FullTimeEmployee and PartTimeEmployee classes both have findPaymentAmount methods, but each class's method works quite differently.

Yes, I have some things for you to try:

BUY OR RENT

In Chapter 9, you create instances of your own PlaceToLive class and display information about those instances. Create two subclasses of your PlaceToLive class: a House class and an Apartment class. Each House object has a mortgage cost (a monthly amount) and a property tax cost (a yearly amount). Each Apartment object has a rental cost (a monthly amount).

A main method creates some houses and some apartments. For each house or apartment, your main method displays the total cost per square foot (or square meter) and the total cost per bedroom, both calculated monthly.

TAX BREAKS

In Chapter 7, you create an Organization class. Each instance of your Organization class has a name, an annual revenue amount, and a boolean value indicating whether the organization is or is not a profit-making organization.

Create a new Organization2 class. Each instance of this new class has only a name and an annual revenue amount. Create two subclasses: Call them the ProfitMakingOrganization class and a NonProfitOrganization class. A profit-making organization pays 10 percent of its revenue in tax, but a nonprofit organization pays only 2 percent of its revenue in tax.

Make a main method that creates ProfitMakingOrganization instances as well as NonProfitOrganization instances while also displaying information about each instance, including the amount of tax the organization pays.

Changing the Payments for Only Some of the Employees

Wouldn't you know it! Some knucklehead in the human resources department offered double pay for overtime to one of your part-time employees. Now word is getting around, and some of the other part-timers want double pay for their overtime work. If this keeps up, you'll end up in the poorhouse, so you need to send out a memo to all the part-time employees, explaining why earning more money is not to their benefit.

In the meantime, you have two kinds of part-time employees — the ones who receive double-pay-for-overtime hours and the ones who don’t — so you need to modify your payroll software. What are your options?

  • Well, you can dig right into the PartTimeEmployee class code, make a few changes, and hope for the best. (Not a good idea!)

  • You can follow the previous section’s advice and create a subclass of the existing PartTimeEmployee class. “But wait,” you say. “The existing PartTimeEmployee class already has a findPaymentAmount method. Do I need some tricky way of bypassing this existing findPaymentAmount method for each double-pay-for-overtime employee?”

    At this point, you can thank your lucky stars that you're doing object-oriented programming in Java. With object-oriented programming, you can create a subclass that overrides the functionality of its parent class. Listing 10-6 has just such a subclass.

LISTING 10-6 Yet Another Subclass

public class PartTimeWithOver extends PartTimeEmployee {

@Override
public double findPaymentAmount(int hours) {

if (hours <= 40) {
return getHourlyRate() * hours;
} else {
return getHourlyRate() * 40 + getHourlyRate() * 2 * (hours - 40);
}
}
}

Figure 10-4 shows the relationship between the code in Listing 10-6 and other pieces of code in this chapter. In particular, PartTimeWithOver is a subclass of a subclass. In object-oriented programming, a chain of this kind is not the least bit unusual. In fact, as subclasses go, this chain is rather short.

The PartTimeWithOver class extends the PartTimeEmployee class, but the PartTimeWithOver picks and chooses what it wants to inherit from the PartTimeEmployee class. Because PartTimeWithOver has its own declaration for the findPaymentAmount method, the PartTimeWithOver class doesn't inherit a findPaymentAmount method from its parent. (See Figure 10-5.)

According to the official terminology, the PartTimeWithOver class overrides its parent class's findPaymentAmount method. If you create an object from the PartTimeWithOver class, that object has the name, jobTitle, hourlyRate, and cutCheck of the PartTimeEmployee class, but the object has the findPaymentAmount method that's defined in Listing 10-6.

A Java annotation

The word @Override in Listing 10-6 is an example of an annotation. A Java annotation tells your computer something about your code. In particular, the @Override annotation in Listing 10-6 tells the Java compiler to be on the lookout for a common coding error. The annotation says, “Make sure that the method immediately following this annotation has the same stuff (the same name, the same parameters, and so on) as one of the methods in the superclass. If not, then display an error message.”

So, in Listing 10-6, if I accidentally type

@Override
public double findPaymentAmount(double hours) {

with double hours instead of int hours, the compiler reminds me that my new findPaymentAmount method doesn't really override anything that's in Listing 10-4.

Java has other kinds of annotations. For a list, visit https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/annotations/predefined.html.

Java's @Override annotation is optional. If you remove the word @Override from Listing 10-6, your code still runs correctly. But the @Override annotation gives your code some added safety. With @Override, the compiler checks to make sure that you're doing something you intend to do (namely, overriding one of the superclass's methods). And with apologies to George Orwell, some types of annotations are less optional than others. You can omit certain annotations from your code only if you're willing to replace the annotation with lots and lots of unannotated Java code.

Using methods from classes and subclasses

If you need clarification on this notion of overriding a method, look at the code in Listing 10-7. A run of that code is shown in Figure 10-6.

LISTING 10-7 Paying Three Kinds of Employees

void main() {
var ftEmployee = new FullTimeEmployee();

ftEmployee.setName("Barry Burd");
ftEmployee.setJobTitle("CEO");
ftEmployee.setWeeklySalary(5000.00);
ftEmployee.setBenefitDeduction(500.00);
ftEmployee.cutCheck(ftEmployee.findPaymentAmount());

var ptEmployee = new PartTimeEmployee();

ptEmployee.setName("Chris Apelian");
ptEmployee.setJobTitle("Computer Book Author");
ptEmployee.setHourlyRate(7.53);
ptEmployee.cutCheck(ptEmployee.findPaymentAmount(50));

var ptoEmployee = new PartTimeWithOver();

ptoEmployee.setName("Steve Surace");
ptoEmployee.setJobTitle("Driver");
ptoEmployee.setHourlyRate(7.53);
ptoEmployee.cutCheck(ptoEmployee.findPaymentAmount(55));
}

The code in Listing 10-7 writes checks to three employees. The first employee is a full-timer. The second is a part-time employee who hasn't yet gotten wind of the overtime payment scheme. The third employee knows about the overtime payment scheme and demands a fair wage.

With the subclasses, all three of these employees coexist in Listing 10-7. Sure, one subclass extends the old PartTimeEmployee class, but that doesn't mean you can’t create an object from the PartTimeEmployee class. In fact, Java is smart about this. Listing 10-7 has three calls to the findPaymentAmount method, and each call reaches out to a different version of the method:

  • In the first call, ftEmployee.findPaymentAmount, the ftEmployee variable is an instance of the FullTimeEmployee class. So the method that's called is the one in Listing 10-2.
  • In the second call, ptEmployee.findPaymentAmount, the ptEmployee variable is an instance of the PartTimeEmployee class. So the method that's called is the one in Listing 10-4.
  • In the third call, ptoEmployee.findPaymentAmount, the ptoEmployee variable is an instance of the PartTimeWithOver class. So the method that's called is the one in Listing 10-6.

This code is fantastic. Using subclasses makes the code clean and elegant. With all the money that you save on software, you can afford to pay everyone double for overtime hours. (Whether you do that or keep the money for yourself is another story.)

In addition to the monthly rental price, someone living in an ApartmentWithFees pays a fixed amount every quarter (every three months). Create a main method that displays the monthly cost of living in a House instance, an Apartment instance, and an ApartmentWithFees instance.

VIRTUAL METHODS

Create a project with four Java source files. Each file defines a particular Java class:

void main() {
MyThing myThing, myThing2;

myThing = new MySubThing();
myThing2 = new MyOtherThing();

myThing.value = 7;
myThing2.value = 44;
myThing.display();
myThing2.display();
}

int value;

public void display() {
System.out.println("In MyThing, value is " + value);
}
}

public class MySubThing extends MyThing {

@Override
public void display() {
System.out.println("In MySUBThing, value is " + value);
}

public class MyOtherThing extends MyThing {

public void display() {

}

What output do you see when you run the Main.java file's code? What does this output tell you about variable declarations and method calling in Java?

THE WAITING GAME

In Chapter 8, you create your own AirplaneFlight class. Create a subclass that has a method named duration. The duration method, which has no parameters, returns the amount of time between the flight's departure time and arrival time.

To find the number of hours between two LocalTime objects (such as twoFifteen and currentTime), execute

long hours = ChronoUnit.HOURS.between(twoFifteen, currentTime);

To find the number of minutes between two LocalTime objects (such as twoFifteen and currentTime), execute

long minutes = ChronoUnit.MINUTES.between(twoFifteen, currentTime);

Yet Another switch

From one version of Java to the next, the switch structure becomes more and more versatile. With Java 23, a switch does almost anything you want it to do. The folks at Wiley don't know it yet, but someday, they'll have to publish a book titled Java's switch Statements and Expressions For Dummies.

Listing 10-8 demonstrates the switch structure's pattern-matching feature.

LISTING 10-8 What Will They Think of Next?

void main() {
var ptEmployee = new PartTimeEmployee();
ptEmployee.setName("Chris Apelian");
ptEmployee.setJobTitle("Computer Book Author");
ptEmployee.setHourlyRate(7.53);
payEmployee(ptEmployee);

var ptoEmployee = new PartTimeWithOver();
ptoEmployee.setName("Steve Surace");
ptoEmployee.setJobTitle("Driver");
ptoEmployee.setHourlyRate(7.53);
payEmployee(ptoEmployee);

var employee = new Employee();
payEmployee(employee);
}

void payEmployee(Employee employee) {
employee.cutCheck(switch (employee) {
case FullTimeEmployee fte -> fte.findPaymentAmount();
case PartTimeWithOver pto -> pto.findPaymentAmount(55);
case PartTimeEmployee pte -> pte.findPaymentAmount(50);
case Employee e -> 0.00;
});
}

When you run the code in Listing 10-8, you get the output shown in Figure 10-7. In Listing 10-8, the employee object has no name and no job title. So, on the last line in Figure 10-7, that person's name and title are both null. In Java, null means “no value.”

The main method in Listing 10-8 calls payEmployee three times. Each time, the payEmployee method dives into a switch expression. Like the switch structures in earlier examples, this switch divides into cases. But unlike those earlier switch structures, this expression's cases are the names of classes. The switch expression asks, “What subclass does the employee parameter belong to?” Depending on the answer, the switch expression calls one of the subclasses' findPaymentAmount methods (or gives up and returns 0.00).

If you mess with the cases in Listing 10-8, you may run into trouble. For example, try changing the order of the middle two cases, like this:

// Bad code with cases reversed!
case PartTimeEmployee pte -> pte.findPaymentAmount(50);
case PartTimeWithOver pto -> pto.findPaymentAmount(55);

Java absolutely despises this code, and lets you know by displaying a harsh message. “Label is dominated by a preceding case label,” says Java. Why does Java say this? I'm glad you asked.

Think about the ptoEmployee object in Listing 10-8. It's an instance of the PartTimeWithOver class. But the PartTimeWithOver class is a subclass of PartTimeEmployee. So ptoEmployee is also an instance of the PartTimeEmployee class. In fact, ptoEmployee is an instance of all three classes — PartTimeWithOver, PartTimeEmployee, and Employee. Java's switch expression looks for a match from the topmost case downward. (See Figure 10-8.) So, in the Cases Reversed code, the ptoEmployee object matches the PartTimeEmployee case and never reaches the PartTimeWithOver case. In fact, nothing ever reaches the PartTimeWithOver case. The PartTimeWithOver case is useless, so Java refuses to accept the code.

Here's another thing you can do to ruin the case expression in Listing 10-8. Try removing the last Employee e case. Java's switch expression must deliver a value no matter what kind of Employee instance you feed to it. But the employee object near the end of the listing's main method matches none of the first three case clauses. So, without the Employee e case, Java makes an unpleasant fuss.

The cases in a switch expression of this kind must cover all possibilities. Even if you remove the last two statements in the main method in Listing 10-8, Java insists on having a case clause that can catch a new Employee() object.

Rather than list every possibility, you can get lazy and end a switch expression with a default clause. Just don't put both the Employee case and a default clause in Listing 10-8. Java would rebel against that, too.

Doing Something about the Weather

Here's some feedback I got from a reader:

  • Hi Barry,
  • In Chapter 8, the way you display a temperature bothers me. Instead of displaying 70.00° FAHRENHEIT, you should display 70 °F. What gives with your crazy temperature notation?
  • All the best,
  • Persnickety Percy

And I replied thusly:

  • Hi Persnickety,
  • To display temperatures your way, create a subclass of my Temperature class. You can find the code in Listing 10-9.
  • Regards,
  • Barry

LISTING 10-9 Persnickety Percy Gets His Way

public class TemperatureForPercy extends Temperature {

public TemperatureForPercy() {
super(); // This super call is optional. (See this
// chapter's "Constructor madness" section.)
}

public TemperatureForPercy(double number) {
super(number);
}

public TemperatureForPercy(TempScale scale) {
super(scale);
}

public TemperatureForPercy(double number, TempScale scale) {
super(number, scale);
}

@Override
public String toString() {
return String.format("%2.0f \u00B0", getNumber()) +
switch (getScale()) {
case CELSIUS -> "C";
case FAHRENHEIT -> "F";
case KELVIN -> "K";
case RANKINE -> "R";

};
}

public double toCelsius() {
return switch (getScale()) {
case CELSIUS -> getNumber();
case FAHRENHEIT -> (getNumber()- 32) * 5.0 / 9.0;
case KELVIN -> getNumber()- 273.15;
case RANKINE -> (getNumber()- 491.67) * 5.0 / 9.0;
};
}
}

In the toString and toCelsius methods of Listing 10-9, notice the calls to the Temperature class's getNumber and getScale methods. Why do I do this? Well, inside the TemperatureForPercy class's code, any direct references to the number and scale fields would generate error messages. It's true that every TemperatureForPercy instance has its own number and scale fields. (After all, TemperatureForPercy is a subclass of the Temperature class, and the code for the Temperature class defines the number and scale fields.) But because number and scale are declared to be private inside the Temperature class, only code that's right inside the Temperature class can directly use these fields.

Don't put additional declarations of the number and scale fields inside the TemperatureForPercy class's code. If you do, you inadvertently create four different variables (two called number and another two called scale). You'll assign values to one pair of variables. Then you'll be shocked that when you display the other pair of variables, those values seem to have disappeared.

When an object’s code contains a call to one of the object’s own methods, you don’t need to preface the call with a dot. For instance, in the toString method of Listing 10-9, the object calls its own methods with getNumber() and getScale(), not with someObject.getNumber() and somethingOrOther.getScale(). If going dotless makes you queasy, you can compensate by taking advantage of yet another use for the this keyword: Just write this.getNumber() and this.getScale() in the toString method in Listing 10-9.

Constructors for subclasses

By far, the biggest news in Listing 10-9 is the way the code declares constructors. The TemperatureForPercy class has four of its own constructors. If you've gotten in gear thinking about subclass inheritance, you may wonder why these constructor declarations are necessary. Doesn't TemperatureForPercy inherit the parent Temperature class's constructors? No, subclasses don't inherit constructors.

Subclasses don’t inherit constructors.

That’s right. Subclasses don’t inherit constructors. The default constructors in Chapter 8 may look as if they're inherited, but they're not. In general, when you define a subclass, you declare new constructors to go with the subclass.

So the code in Listing 10-9 has four constructors. Each constructor has the name TemperatureForPercy, and each constructor has its own uniquely identifiable parameter list. That’s the boring part. The interesting part is that each constructor makes a call to something named super, which is a Java keyword.

In Listing 10-9, super stands for a constructor in the parent class:

  • The statement super() in Listing 10-9 calls the parameterless Temperature() constructor that's in Listing 8-2. (Yes, you'll need to flip back to Chapter 8 to find it.) That parameterless constructor assigns 0.0 to the number field and TempScale.FAHRENHEIT to the scale field.
  • The statement super(number, scale) in Listing 10-9 calls the constructor Temperature(double number, TempScale scale) that's in Listing 8-2. In turn, the constructor assigns values to the number and scale fields.
  • In a similar way, the statements super(number) and super(scale) in Listing 10-9 call constructors from Listing 8-2.

The computer decides which of the Temperature class's constructors is being called by looking at the parameter list after the word super. For instance, when the computer executes

super(number, scale);

from Listing 10-9, the computer says to itself, “The number and scale fields in parentheses have types double and TempScale. And only one of the Temperature constructors in Listing 8-2 has two parameters with types double and TempScale. The constructor's header looks like this:

public Temperature(double number, TempScale scale)

“So I guess I'll execute the statements inside that particular constructor.”

Using all this stuff

In Listing 10-9, I define what it means to be in the TemperatureForPercy class. Now it’s time to put this TemperatureForPercy class to good use. Listing 10-10 has code that uses TemperatureForPercy.

LISTING 10-10 Using Percy's Class

void main() {
println(new TemperatureForPercy(2.73, TempScale.KELVIN));
println(new TemperatureForPercy(TempScale.CELSIUS));
println(new TemperatureForPercy(32.0));

var temperature = new TemperatureForPercy();
temperature.setNumber(70);
println(temperature);
}

Listing 10-10 creates instances of the TemperatureForPercy class, so the listing's println calls access the toString method in the TemperatureForPercy class, not the parent Temperature class.

Figure 10-9 shows a run of the code in Listing 10-10.

Read the comment after the first super call in Listing 10-9. Try removing that super call and notice that you still get the output shown in Figure 10-9. What does this tell you? It tells you that, under certain circumstances, Java adds a parameterless super() call to your constructor.

And what are those “certain circumstances”? The next section reveals the answer.

Constructor madness

The big message in the previous section is that subclasses don't inherit constructors. When you combine this with some other rules concerning constructors, you get some surprising outcomes. Here are some facts about constructors:

  1. A subclass doesn't inherit any constructors from its parent class.

  2. When you define a class, and you don't explicitly type the code for any constructors, Java generates a parameterless default constructor for you.

    This rule goes both ways. If you explicitly type the code for a constructor, Java doesn't generate a default constructor for you.

  3. When a class contains a constructor, and that constructor doesn't contain a statement of this kind:

    super(some parameters or no parameters);

    then Java generates a parameterless super() call for you. In other words, Java calls the parent class's parameterless constructor on your behalf.

To see these rules in action, consider the code in Listings 10-11 through 10-13.

LISTING 10-11 Getting Help in the Kitchen

public class KitchenItem {
public String purpose;

public KitchenItem() {
System.out.println("""
You've called the parameterless
KitchenItem constructor.""");
}
}

LISTING 10-12 Don't Eat with Your Hands

enum Material {METAL, PLASTIC, WOOD}

public class Utensil extends KitchenItem {
public Material material;

public Utensil(String purpose, Material material) {
this.purpose = purpose;
this.material = material;
}

// Some code is missing.
}

LISTING 10-13 You May Have to Google the Word Tine

public class Fork extends Utensil {
public int numberOfTines;
}

If you type all this code, Listing 10-13 gives you an error message such as, There is no default constructor available in 'Utensil'. Why is Java complaining to you? Have you done something wrong? Figure 10-10 illustrates the situation.

With Rules 2 and 3, an implicit default constructor inside the Fork class tries to call a parameterless Utensil constructor. But Rule 2 tells Java not to create a parameterless Utensil constructor. So the super() in the Fork class's default constructor has nothing to call. Java recognizes this difficulty and insists that you repair your code.

You can fix this by adding an explicit parameterless constructor to the Utensil class in Listing 10-12:

public class Utensil extends KitchenItem {
public Material material;

public Utensil(String purpose, Material material) {
this.purpose = purpose;
this.material = material;
}

public Utensil() {
}
}

Figure 10-11 shows you what happens when you add this constructor.

In Figure 10-11, a call to the Fork class's default constructor sets off a chain of calls that ends with a call to the KitchenItem constructor. Normally, you don't put println calls of any kind inside a constructor declaration. But in this example, the println I've added helps to convince you that Java obeys Rules 2 and 3.

Here's a neat little program for you to write:

A CONVERSION DIVERSION

You may have noticed that the TemperatureForPercy class in Listing 10-9 has a toCelsius method. Create a subclass of TemperatureForPercy named TemperatureCelsius. The TemperatureCelsius class has only three constructors. When you run this main method:

void main() {
println(new TemperatureCelsius());

println(new TemperatureCelsius(100.00));

var temp = new TemperatureForPercy(70.0, TempScale.FAHRENHEIT);
println(new TemperatureCelsius(temp));
}

the output is

0 °C
100 °C
21 °C

Improving your batting average

Our family's neighborhood elementary school has a yearly tradition: Each spring, the students in fifth grade take a daylong field trip to Philadelphia. When my son was in fifth grade, I went along on the trip to help supervise 4 of the 20 children. While the 4 kids and I were touring the city's historical sites, I misplaced the preplanned itinerary. I didn't know where we were supposed to go next. So, what could I do? I did what any good Philadelphia native would do — I ignored the itinerary and took the kids to the nearest cheap restaurant. I treated them all to Philadelphia's signature dish — the fat-laden, greasy, Philadelphia cheesesteak.

What could this story possibly have to do with Java? That's simple. This chapter is about access — how one class's code may gain access to another class's code. My Philadelphia anecdote is about access, too. Shortly after the school trip, my son's fifth-grade teacher got wind of my shenanigans during the tour. Later, when my daughter was in fifth grade, the teacher said that I wasn’t welcome to take part in that year's junket to Philadelphia. The teacher had revoked my access to those Philadelphia cheesesteaks.

Making a Package

Today, our local baseball team plays against the neighboring town's team. Our team is the Hankies; the other town's team is the Socks. As the team's official recordkeeper, I've created code to keep track of the players' names and batting averages. (See Listing 11-1.)

LISTING 11-1 The Player Record Class

package com.example.baseball;

public record Player(String name, double average) {
}

Wow! That's a tiny piece of code! (If you have doubts about what's going on in Listing 11-1, refer to the section on record classes in Chapter 8.) To sum it up, each Player instance has a name field and an average field. There's only one way to create a Player instance, and that's by calling new Player(a_name, an_average). Once you've created a player, you can't change that player's name or average. To get a particular player's name and average, you call the record class's name() and average() methods. That's all there is to it.

For comparison, the Player class in previous editions of Java For Dummies looked something like this:

public class Player {
String name;
double average;

public Player(String name, double average) {
this.name = name;
this.average = average;
}
}

This older code did mostly what the code in Listing 11-1 does.

Package deal

The Player class in Listing 11-1 belongs to a package that I named com.example.baseball. The first line in Listing 11-1 makes it so. That first line is called a package declaration. That line says, “This file is one of possibly many files that are grouped inside a package named com.example.baseball.”

In Java, every class belongs to a package. Imagine a file named Hello.java containing only this text:

void main() {
println("Hello");
}

Because of the file's name, this main method belongs to an implicit class named Hello. And that Hello class belongs to an implicit package. Java developers call it an unnamed package.

None of the listings in previous chapters starts with a package declaration, so each of those listings belongs to an unnamed package. But professional Java programmers avoid using unnamed packages. So, in Listing 11-1, I decided to straighten up and start flying right.

The Java API defines thousands of classes, each belonging to one of several hundred packages. When you write import java.util.Scanner, you're referring to a class named Scanner, which belongs to the package java.util.

In the Java world, programmers customarily give packages long, dot-filled names. For example, I've registered the domain name allmycode.com, so I may decide to name a package com.allmycode.dummiesframe. In truth, I can name a package almost anything I want — like com.example.baseball, fish.and.chips, or simply hamburger. In any case, informative package names like com.allmycode.dummiesframe are better than silly names like midnight.in.akron or do.not.run.this.code.

In this book, I start most of my package names with com.example. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority has set aside the example.com domain for anyone to use in writing documentation, illustrating concepts, describing ideas, and so on.

How many classes can you define? The Player class in Listing 11-1 is one of them. You can also create a Game class, a Season class, and classes named Inning, Bat, Ball, Strike, HomeRun, Foul, Base, Pitcher, Catcher, Umpire, Manager, Infielder, Outfielder, DoublePlay, and many more. Of course, you may want to separate these classes from your other classes named Song, Novel, Film, Painting, and Video. So you might create two different packages: one named com.example.baseball and another named com.example.arts.

You can start any Java file with a package declaration, but you have to remember a few things:

  • A Java file's package name dictates the names of some folders and subfolders.

    The code in Listing 11-1 begins with package com.example.baseball. So your hard drive must have a folder named com, which has a subfolder named example, which in turn has its own subfolder named baseball. Your Player.java file must be inside this baseball folder. For example, on my computer, I have a project whose root folder is named 11-01. My copy of Listing 11-1 is inside the 11-01/src/com/example/baseball folder.

  • Many IDEs have to be told explicitly to create the needed folders.

    Before you copy the code from Listing 11-1 into your IDE, you probably have to tell the IDE to create a package named com.example.baseball. When you do, your IDE will create the com/example/baseball folders for you. Then you can copy the Player.java file into the com/example/baseball folder.

    How do you tell your IDE to create a package? When you start a new project, your IDE might prompt you for a new package name. The IDE creates the package as part of the new project. When you work on an existing project, creating a package might mean fishing around for New ⇒   Package among your IDE's menus. If you can't find a way to do that, look for some hints on this book's website (http://javafordummies.allmycode.com).

After all this fuss about packages, you may wonder what difference it makes that a class is in one package or another. For some insight, see this chapter's later section “It's All About Access.”

Using the Player class

Listing 11-2 has code that uses the Player class — the class that's defined earlier, in Listing 11-1.

LISTING 11-2 Using the Player Class

import com.example.baseball.Player;

import java.io.*;
import java.util.Scanner;

public class ShowPlayers {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
var hankiesData = new Scanner(new File("Hankies.txt"));

IO.print("Player");
IO.println(String.format("%45s", "Batting Average"));
IO.print("------");
IO.println(String.format("%45s", "---------------"));

for (int num = 1; num <= 9; num++) {
var player = new Player(hankiesData.nextLine(),
hankiesData.nextDouble());
hankiesData.nextLine();
IO.print(String.format("%-40s", player.name()));
IO.println(String.format("%.3f", player.average()).substring(1));
}

hankiesData.close();
}
}

WHAT'S ALL THE FUSS ABOUT?

Would you like to see a simple source file replacement for the code Listing 11-2? Well, here it is:

import com.example.baseball.Player;

void main() throws IOException {
var hankiesData = new Scanner(new File("Hankies.txt"));

print("Player");
println(String.format("%45s", "Batting Average"));
print("------");
println(String.format("%45s", "---------------"));

for (int num = 1; num <= 9; num++) {
var player = new Player(hankiesData.nextLine(),
hankiesData.nextDouble());
hankiesData.nextLine();
print(String.format("%-40s", player.name()));
println(String.format("%.3f", player.average()).substring(1));
}

hankiesData.close();
}

Here's how this simple source file differs from the code in Listing 11-2:

  • In this code, you don't explicitly create a class to contain the main method. Instead, Java implicitly defines a containing class for you.
  • Implicitly declared classes automatically import everything inside the java.base module. In this sidebar's code, you don't have to write import declarations for java.io and java.util because both of these packages are in the java.base module.
  • Sorry! You need an explicit import declaration for com.example.baseball.Player. The people who decide what's part of the Java API didn't create the com.example.baseball.Player class. I did.
  • In this sidebar's code, you can skip public static and String[] args. With their infinite kindness, the lords of Java 23 have deemed these words to be unnecessary.
  • In this code, you don't have to preface the print and println calls with IO. When you create an implicitly declared class, Java imagines that you've written static import declarations for these methods. (Well, wha' da' ya' know? There's a section titled “All about static import” in this very chapter!)
  • With this sidebar's code, you still have to use the Scanner class to read values. You can't use the simpler readln method because readln gets values only from the keyboard. In this example, you read from a disk file.

This sidebar's code has a few brand-new features, and so does Listing 11-2. You can read about these features in the pages that follow.

In a typical Java application, the application's classes belong to several different packages. And the code in those packages depends on code from other organizations' packages. Examples like the ones in this book, with only one or two packages, are rare indeed.

For my baseball example, I put the Player class in a package that I name com.example.baseball and put the ShowPlayers class in Java's ever-present unnamed package. Since the ShowPlayers class isn't in the same package as my Player class, I start Listing 11-2 with an import declaration. Without the import declaration at the very top of Listing 11-2, I'd have to write

var player = new com.example.baseball.Player(hankiesData.nextLine(),
hankiesData.nextDouble());

inside the listing's for loop.

In Listing 11-2, notice how import java.io.*; ends with an asterisk. The asterisk means “import every class that's in the java.io package.” Listing 11-2 abbreviates three of those classes: IOException, File, and IO. But, with an asterisk in the import declaration, the listing could abbreviate BufferedReader, FileInputStream, or any other classes in the java.io package.

A Java package can have one or more subpackages. For example, the javax.swing.text package is for displaying text of any kind in a graphical window, and the javax.swing.text.html subpackage is for displaying HTML text in particular. But don't let the name subpackage fool you. The relationship between a package and its subpackage is flimsy. If you declare import javax.swing.text.*, you can abbreviate the names of classes in the javax.swing.text package — classes like Caret, Highlighter, Position, and Style. But you can't abbreviate the names of classes in the javax.swing.text.html package. For that, you declare import javax.swing.text.html.*.

Running the code

To run this program, you need a file containing data on your favorite baseball players. Fortunately, the stuff you download from this book's website comes with a Hankies.txt file. (See Figure 11-1.)

For a run of the code in Listing 11-2, see Figure 11-2.

The program's Hankies.txt file can't be in just any old folder on your computer's hard drive. The file has to be in a place where Java can find it, which is most likely your project's root folder. If Java can't find the file, then a run of this section's example gives you an unpleasant FileNotFoundException message. For advice on choosing locations for files like Hankies.txt, refer to Chapters 6 and 9.

You may live in a country where the value of π is approximately 3,14159 (with a comma) instead of 3.14159 (with a period). If you do, the file shown in Figure 11-1 won't work for you. The program will crash with an InputMismatchException. To run this section's example, you have to change the periods in the Hankies.txt file into commas. Alternatively, you can add a statement such as Locale.setDefault(Locale.US) to your code. For details, see Chapter 9.

For this section's code to work correctly, you must have a line break after the last .212 in Figure 11-1. For details about line breaks, see Chapter 9.

One class; nine objects

The code in Listing 11-2 calls the Player constructor nine times. The result is that the code creates nine instances of the Player class. The first time through the loop, the code creates an instance with the name Barry Burd. The second time through the loop, the code abandons the Barry Burd instance and creates another instance with name Harriet Ritter. The third time through, the code abandons poor Harriet Ritter and creates an instance for Weelie J. Katz. The code has only one instance at a time but, all in all, the code creates nine instances.

Each Player instance has its own name and average fields. Each instance also has its own Player constructor and, since it's a record class, its own name() and average() methods. Look at Figure 11-3 and think of the Player class with its nine incarnations.

Some notes on formatting

Figure 11-4 illustrates the work of the first two printing statements in Listing 11-2. In "%45s", the letter s says, “Expect the next parameter to be a string.” And the next parameter, "Batting Average", is indeed a string. In that same code, the number 45 says “Use 45 characters to display the string.” So Java pads the 15-character "Batting Average" string with 30 blank spaces.

Figure 11-5 shows how a print call in Listing 11-2 formats my favorite player's name. In "%-40s", the 40s says, “Use 40 characters to display the second parameter, which is a string.” The minus sign calls for left-justification, so the name is to the left of the 30-character padding.

Figure 11-6 describes the formatting of a player's batting average. In "%.3f", the .3f part asks for a number with three digits to the right of the decimal point. For numbers less than 1, Java puts a digit 0 on the left side of the decimal point. That's usually good. (My high-school teacher told me to do that so that the decimal point would be harder to miss.)

But the convention for displaying batting averages is to not have this leading 0. So, to get rid of the leading 0, I call Java's substring method. In particular,

  • The value of "0.101".substring(0) is "0.101",
  • The value of "0.101".substring(1) is ".101",
  • The value of “0.101”.substring(2) is “101”,

… and so on.

Calling String.format isn't the only way to format numbers in Java. Other ways include the System.out.printf method, the DecimalFormat class, and the NumberFormat class's getCurrencyInstance method. For more information, see Chapter 12.

MEN'S CLOTHING

A line of men's clothing features shirts, pants, jackets, overcoats, neckties, and shoes. Create an enum to represent the six kinds of items. Then create a MensClothingItem class. Each instance of the class has a kind (one of the six enum values) and a name (such as Casual Summer Design #7).

Write code to display a table with six rows that describe one complete men's wardrobe.

DEAL ME IN

Create an enum to represent the suits in a deck of playing cards (CLUBS, DIAMONDS, HEARTS, and SPADES). Create a PlayingCard class. Each playing card has a number (from 1 to 13) and a suit. In the numbering scheme, 11 stands for a Jack, 12 stands for a Queen, and 13 stands for a King. Write code that creates several cards and displays them on the screen.

It's All About Access

Many examples in this book throw around the words public and private as if they're no big deal at all. That's okay because the English-language meanings of the words describe, more or less, what they mean in a Java program. But it's nice to be precise. So this section zooms in on the words public and private. These words are two of Java's access modifiers. The word protected is another Java access modifier. And, not using any word (in a place where you can use public, private, or protected) is also a kind of access modifier.

For starters, what does access mean? Imagine that you have two fields, two methods, a class with a separate method, or two things of any kind. Does the name of the first thing mean anything to the second thing? Here are two pieces of code:

class First {
int number = 0;
}

class Second {
void main() {
var first = new First();
first.number = 99;
}
}

Is this code okay? Can the Second class's main method refer to the First class and to its number field? If so, the Second class has access to these things.

An access modifier helps to determine what kind of access is available. To describe Java's access modifiers, I start with the big picture — modules.

Access for Java modules

There's an old poem that goes something like this:

As I was going to high school,
I ran some code with seven modules,
Each module had seven packages,
Each package had seven classes,
Each class had seven members:
Members, classes, packages, and modules,
How many were there going to high school?

A module is a group of packages. Each module is a world unto itself. If you have two modules and you don't do anything to connect the two modules, then none of the code in either module can make reference to code in the other module.

Imagine that you have two modules: module1 and module2. If you want some code in module2 to make reference to any of the code in module1, then module1 must explicitly export the code, and module2 must explicitly require the code. You must create two files, both named module-info.java, like so:

// One module-info.java file:
module module1 {
exports some_package_in_module1;
}

// Another module-info.java file:
module module2 {
requires some_package_in_module1;
}

The details can be complicated. But that's okay because most Java programmers never have to create modules. In other words, you're off the hook.

For more information about modules, visit https://openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/quick-start.

From this point on in the chapter, wherever you read about “two packages” or “two classes,” imagine that they're both in the same module.

Access modifiers for classes

In Java, the public keyword has two slightly different meanings: one meaning for the members of a class and another meaning for the classes themselves. This section deals with the classes themselves.

A class can be either public or nonpublic. If you see something like

public class Drawing

you're looking at the declaration of a public class. But if you see plain old

class OnlyMyDrawing

the class that's being declared isn’t public.

Public classes

If a class is public, you can refer to the class from anywhere in your code. Of course, some restrictions apply. You must obey all the rules in this chapter’s earlier sections “Package deal” and “Access for Java modules.” You must also refer to a packaged class properly. For example, in Listing 11-2, you write

import com.example.baseball.Player;

var player = new Player(hankiesData.nextLine(),
hankiesData.nextDouble());

Alternatively, you can do without the import declaration and write

var player = new com.example.baseball.Player(hankiesData.nextLine(),
hankiesData.nextDouble());

One way or another, your code must acknowledge that the Player class isn't in the same package as the code in Listing 11-2.

Nonpublic classes

If a class isn't public, you can refer to the class only from code within the class’s package.

I tested this rule. I went back to Listing 11-1 and deleted the word public. At that point, Listing 11-2 went poof! To be more precise, my IDE displayed these messages for Listing 11-2:

'com.example.baseball.Player' is not public in 'com.example.baseball'.
Cannot be accessed from outside package.
Cannot access 'name()' in 'com.example.baseball.Player.
Cannot access 'average()' in 'com.example.baseball.Player."

I guess I got what was coming to me.

Things are never as simple as they seem. The rules I describe in this section apply to almost every class in this book. But Java has fancy things called sealed classes and inner classes, and these classes follow a different set of rules. Fortunately, a typical novice programmer has little contact with sealed or inner classes. So, for now, you can live quite happily with the rules that I describe in this section.

Enough about access rules for classes! It's time to explore other avenues.

A word or two about method-local variables

Consider this chunk of Java code:

public class MyClass {
int myField; // This is a field (a member of MyClass).
// myVariable++; // Illegal. No access.

void myMethod() { // This is a method (another member of MyClass).
int myVariable; // This is a method-local variable (NOT a member).
}
}

The comments on the right side of the code tell the whole story. This class has three kinds of members: a field, a method, and a method-local variable. There's not much to say about method-local variables. A method-local variable can't be accessed from any code outside of the method. Period. If you want more details, refer to Chapter 7.

Access for members (fields and methods)

Imagine for a moment that you're a member of a class. In particular, you're a field named identificationNumber. From somewhere in the code, you hear the words “Hey, identificationNumber! What's your current value?” Your first response should be, “Who wants to know?” Depending on who's asking for the identificationNumber, you may or may not be willing to answer.

Members in the same class

Two members in the same class have free and easy access to one another. For example, the following code is right and proper:

class MyClass {
private int x = 7;
private int y = addOne();

private int addOne() {
return x + 1;
}

void main() {
System.out.println(y);
}
}

The output of this silly program is 8. In this program, every name is available to the rest of the program's code. The addOne method uses the value of x, the initialization of y calls addOne, and main uses the value of y. Almost everything is declared to be private. But because everything is in the same class, the word private doesn't matter.

Members in different classes

The ability to access a member of a different class depends on that member's access modifier. Here's the whole story:

PRIVATE ACCESS

If a member is private, only code that's inside the member’s class can refer directly to that member’s name. Here's some sample code:

class SomeClass {
private int myField = 10;
}

///////////////////////////////

class SomeOtherClass {

void main() {
var someObject = new SomeClass();
System.out.println(someObject.myField); //This doesn't work.
}
}

For a picture that describes private access, see Figure 11-7.

PUBLIC ACCESS

If a member is public, any code can refer directly to that member’s name. Here's some sample code:

class SomeClass {
public int myField = 10;
}

///////////////////////////////

class SomeOtherClass {

void main() {
var someObject = new SomeClass();

System.out.println(someObject.myField); //This works.
}
}

(Remember that both classes have to be in the same module. Otherwise, all bets are off.) For a picture that describes public access, see Figure 11-8.

Public fields are easy to use and even easier to misuse. The best way to engineer your code is to make access to each field as restrictive as possible. If a field doesn't absolutely need to be public, try making it private. If other classes have to get or set the field's values, provide public getter and setter methods.

DEFAULT ACCESS

A member declared without any of the words public, private, or protected in front of it has default access, also known as package-wide access. A member with default access is accessible only in the package in which its class resides. Figure 11-9 illustrates the point.

A subpackage has no more access than any other package. Think about two packages: com.burdbrain.drawings and com.burdbrain.drawings.rectangles. One is a subpackage of the other. One lives in a com/burdbrain/drawings folder with the other in the com/burdbrain/drawings/rectangles folder. Can these packages access each other's default members? You might guess that they can. But no, they can't. A package and its subpackage have the same privileges as two unrelated packages. That's the shocking truth.

PROTECTED ACCESS

When I was first getting to know Java, I thought the word protected meant “nice and secure” or something like that. “Wow, that field is protected. It must be hard to get at.” Well, this notion turned out to be wrong. In Java, a member that's protected is less hidden, less secure, and available for use in more classes than one that has default access. In other words, protected access is more permissive than default access. For me, the terminology is misleading. But that's the way it is.

Think of protected access this way: You start with a field that has default access (a field without the word public, private, or protected in its declaration). That field can be accessed only inside its own package. Now add the word protected to the front of the field's declaration. Suddenly, some classes outside that field's package have access to the field. You can now reference the field from a subclass of the class in which the field is declared. You can also reference the field from a sub-subclass, a sub-sub-subclass, and so on. Any descendant class will do. Figure 11-10 has the story.

Don't stress your brain trying to understand protected access. You can read about it again if you ever need to know about it.

Here are some things for you to try:

NAME THAT TUNE

A Work has a title (a String) and a release year (an int).

The Song and Painting classes are subclasses of the Work class. Each Song instance has a genre (a value from an enum named Genre). The values of Genre are ROCK, POP, BLUES, and CLASSICAL. Each Painting instance has a style (a value from an enum named Style). The values of Style are REALISTIC, ABSTRACT, IMPRESSIONISM, and EXPRESSIONISM.

Each Artist instance has a name (a String) and a Work instance.

Create these classes. Devise a plausible scenario in which these classes would be spread over more than one package. In a separate class, construct instances of each class, and display information about these instances on the screen.

WHAT'S MINE IS YOURS
