The following four classes live in four different .java files. Without typing these classes in an IDE's editor, decide which statements will cause the IDE to display error messages. For each such statement, decide on the least permissive access change that would eliminate the error message:


// THIS CODE DOES NOT COMPILE:

package com.mypackage.things;

import com.yourpackage.stuff.Stuff;
import com.yourpackage.stuff.morestuff.MoreStuff;

public class Things {
protected int i = 0;
private int j = 0;
int k = 0;

public static void main(String[] args) {
var stuff = new Stuff();
System.out.println(stuff.i);
var moreStuff = new MoreStuff();
System.out.println(moreStuff.i);
}
}

package com.yourpackage.stuff;

import com.yourpackage.stuff.morestuff.MoreStuff;

public class Stuff {
protected int i = 0;

void aMethod() {
new MoreStuff().myMethod();
}
}

package com.yourpackage.stuff.morestuff;

import com.mypackage.things.Things;

public class MoreStuff extends Things {
protected void myMethod() {
System.out.println(i);
}
}

package com.mypackage.things;

public class MoreThings extends Things {

public void anotherMethod() {
System.out.println(i);
System.out.println(j);
System.out.println(k);
}
}

Making Static (Finding the Team Average)

Thinking about the code in Listings 11-1 and 11-2, you decide that you want to find the team's overall batting average. Rather than pore over game logs and do a careful analysis, you settle on finding the average of the numbers in Figure 11-2. That's the average of the players' averages. Using this strategy, the team in Figure 11-2 has an average of about .106. No doubt about it: The Hankies need some intensive training.

While the players are out practicing on the ball field, you have a philosophical question to answer. Where should the variables storing your overall, team-average tally go? Should you add more fields to the Player class in Listing 11-1? After considering this possibility, you have some reservations. An instance of the Player class represents just one player on the team. What business does a single player have storing overall team data? Sure, you could make the code work, but it wouldn't be an elegant solution to the problem.

Luckily for you, Java has its static keyword. Anything that's declared to be static belongs to the whole class, not to any particular instance of the class. When you create the static field, totalOfAverages, you create just one copy of the field. This copy stays with the entire class. No matter how many instances of the class you create — one, nine, or none — you have just one totalOfAverages field. And, while you're at it, you create another static field (playerCount) and a static method (findTeamAverage). To see what I mean, look at Figure 11-11.

The Player class in Listing 11-1 does what it was originally supposed to do. And you remember the old saying, “If something's not broken, don't fix it.” With that in mind, you create a brand-new Player class and put it in Listing 11-3. The new Player class has all the features of your old Player class plus a few more.

LISTING 11-3 Creating a Team Batting Average

package com.example.sport;

public record Player(String name, double average) {

private static int playerCount = 0;
private static double totalOfAverages = .000;

public Player {
playerCount++;
totalOfAverages += average;
}

public static double findTeamAverage() {
return totalOfAverages / playerCount;
}
}

Full disclosure: In previous editions of Java For Dummies, the Player class in Listing 11-1 wasn't a record class. But in this edition, I decided to make it a record class. I did this because a 4-line record class saves space on the page. (I also wanted to show off Java's new record class feature.) Anyway, one consequence of this decision is that the code in Listing 11-3 can't extend the Player class in Listing 11-1. Record classes are final. That means you can't create a subclass of a record class. So Listing 11-3 has a completely new Player class. This new Player class has all the features of the old Player class (see Listing 11-1) plus the ability to calculate the overall team average. The two Player classes (see Listings 11-1 and 11-3) are in different packages, so Java won't mistake one of them for the other.

So much static!

In Listing 11-3, I declare playerCount to be static. That's good because something like playerCount (the number of team members) shouldn't belong to individual team members, and having each Player instance keep track of its own count would be silly. (“I know how many team members I am. I'm just one team member!”) If you had nine individual playerCount fields, either each field would store the number 1 (which is useless) or you would have nine different copies of the count, which is wasteful and prone to error. By making playerCount static, you're keeping the playerCount in just one place, where it belongs.

The same kind of reasoning holds for the totalOfAverages. Eventually, the totalOfAverages field will store the sum of the players' batting averages. For all nine members of the Hankies, this adds up to .956.

It's not until someone calls the findTeamAverage method that the computer actually finds the overall Hankies team batting average. You want this findTeamAverage method to be static. Without the word static, there would be nine findTeamAverage methods — one for each instance of the Player class. This wouldn't make much sense. Each instance would have the code to calculate totalOfAverages / playerCount on its own, and each of the nine calculations would yield the same answer.

In general, any task that all instances have in common (and that yields the same result for each instance) should be coded as a static method.

Meet the compact constructor

To find the average of the team members' batting averages, you divide the total of all team members' averages by the number of team members. In Listing 11-3, that's totalOfAverages / playerCount. The playerCount and totalOfAverages fields in Listing 11-3 are static. Whether you have one team member, nine team members, or a thousand team members, there's only one copy of the playerCount field and one copy of the totalOfAverages field.

How do you keep tallies of playerCount and totalOfAverages values? One way is to update these fields whenever you call the Player constructor. If Player wasn't a record class, you'd code a constructor like this:

// A four-statement constructor

public Player(String name, double average) {
this.name = name;
this.average = average;
playerCount++;
totalOfAverages += average;
}

You could do this in Listing 11-3. But since Listing 11-3 is a record class, there's a better way. Remember: When you don't code a constructor in a record class, Java quietly adds its own fully parameterized implicit constructor. In other words, the code in Listing 11-3 automatically gets a constructor of the following kind:

public Player(String name, double average) {
this.name = name;
this.average = average;
}

To this implicit constructor, you want to add a playerCount++ statement and a totalOfAverages += average statement.

Lo and behold! The wizards who design Java thought about your needs! They said you can put a compact constructor in your record class. In Listing 11-3, the compact constructor looks like this:

public Player {
playerCount++;
totalOfAverages += average;
}

A record class's compact constructor has no parentheses after the class's name. When Java sees this, it adds the statements in the compact constructor to the statements in its own implicit constructor. It's as if you had coded this section's 4-statement constructor. That's pretty handy.

Displaying the overall team average

Listing 11-3, shown previously, contains code that defines a Player class, and Listing 11-4 contains code that uses this Player class.

LISTING 11-4 Using the Code from Listing 11-3

import com.example.sport.Player;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.Scanner;

import static java.lang.System.out;

void main() throws IOException {
var hankiesData = new Scanner(new File("Hankies.txt"));

printTableHeader();

for (int num = 1; num <= 9; num++) {
var player = new Player(hankiesData.nextLine(),
hankiesData.nextDouble());
hankiesData.nextLine();
printTableRow(player);
}
hankiesData.close();

printTableSummary();
}

void printTableHeader() {
out.print("Team Member");
out.println(String.format("%40s", "Batting Average"));
out.print("-----------");
out.println(String.format("%40s", "---------------"));
}

void printTableRow(Player player) {
out.print(String.format("%-40s", player.name()));
out.println(String.format("%.3f", player.average()).substring(1));
}

void printTableSummary() {
out.println(String.format("%44s", "----"));
var teamAverageString = String.format("%.3f",
Player.findTeamAverage()).substring(1);
out.println(String.format("%44s", teamAverageString));
}

Figure 11-12 shows a run of the code from Listing 11-4. This run depends on the availability of the Hankies.txt file from Figure 11-1.

Listing 11-4 is rather long, but most of it is the kind of code you see in previous examples.

All about static import

Here's one new and exciting thing in Listing 11-4. It's the listing's import static declaration:

import static java.lang.System.out;

When I add this import static declaration, I can abbreviate the long-winded System.out.print and System.out.println calls.

Other import declarations begin with only the word static. So, why do I need the two words import static for a declaration in Listing 11-4?

The answer is that you can import two kinds of things — classes and static members. The java.util package has a class named Scanner. So, to abbreviate java.util.Scanner with plain old Scanner, you write

import java.util.Scanner;

But the System class (inside the java.lang package) has a static member named out:

public class System {
// …
public static PrintStream out;
}

So, to abbreviate java.lang.System.out with plain old out, you write

import static java.lang.System.out;

You can always abbreviate java.lang.System with the simple name System. Java adds an implicit import java.lang.*; to every program.

All about static references

Notice the code

Player.findTeamAverage()

near the end of Listing 11-4.

That code has the following form:

ClassName.methodName()

In earlier chapters, I say that you normally preface a method call with an object's name, not a class’s name. So why does this dot notation use a class name? The answer: When you call a static method, you preface the method’s name with the name of the class that contains the method. The same holds true whenever you reference another class’s static field. This makes sense because a static member belongs to an entire class, not to any particular instance of the class.

This rule about calling static methods isn't new. Chapter 7 introduces String.format as a way of making output look nice. When I wrote that chapter, I hoped you wouldn't notice that String is the name of a class, not the name of an object. But now, I can come clean. The format method is a static member of the String class.

public class String {
public static String format( … ) {
// …
}
// …
}

So there! To refer to the static format method, you start with the name of the method's class. You write String.format.

Why static members don't always play well with others

In Java, every method must be a member of a class, even if that class is declared implicitly. And before Java 21, every main method had to be static. To honor that tradition, the main method in Listing 11-2 is a static member of a class named ShowPlayers.

public class ShowPlayers {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

As you travel through Javaland, you'll see many static main methods. The thing to remember about static main methods is what other methods they can and cannot call. Take, for example, the following bad code:

// Kids, don't try this at home (or anywhere else).

public class Attendee {

public static void main(String args[]) {
var person1 = new Attendee();
var person2 = new Attendee();
var person3 = new Attendee();
areYouHere();
startMeeting();
}

public void areYouHere() {
System.out.println("I'm here.");
}

public void startMeeting() {
System.out.println("Welcome, everyone.");
}
}

In this bad code, the main method creates three people, tries to ask whether they're attending the meeting, and then tries to start the meeting. The error message I get with this code is “Non-static method cannot be referenced from a static context.” When I first started writing Java programs, I had recurring dreams about seeing this error message. So often did I see this message, so thoroughly was I perplexed, that the memory of this error message became burned into my brain.

In this Attendee class, the main method is static, but the youAreHere and startMeeting methods aren't static. (See Figure 11-13.) So there's only one main method, but there are three versions of the areYouHere method and three versions of the startMeeting method. When the one-and-only main method tries to call areYouHere(), Java doesn't know which instance's areYouHere method to call. The same thing happens when the static main method tries to call startMeeting(). In both cases, Java says “Non-static method cannot be referenced from a static context.”

To find out who's present at a meeting, you don't stare into space and ask “Are you here?” of no one in particular. Instead, you go down your list of people on the roster and ask each of them individually “Are you here?” So each areYouHere call should refer to a specific attendee.

In contrast, starting the formal proceedings is a one-person job. Your code should have only one copy of the startMeeting method, so startMeeting should be static.

Here's some code with the appropriate fixes:

public class Attendee {

public static void main(String args[]) {
var person1 = new Attendee();
var person2 = new Attendee();
var person3 = new Attendee();
person1.areYouHere();
person2.areYouHere();
person3.areYouHere();
startMeeting();
}

public void areYouHere() {
System.out.println("I'm here.");
}

public static void startMeeting() {
System.out.println("Welcome, everyone.");
}
}

The startMeeting method is a static member of the Attendee class. So, instead of calling startMeeting(), you have the option of calling Attendee.startMeeting(). This Attendee prefix is necessary when you want to call the Attendee class's startMeeting method from code that's not inside the Attendee class itself. (Oddly enough, a call like person1.startMeeting() also works, although I've never understood why that way of calling a static method makes any sense.)

I don't know about you, but I can always use some practice with static variables and methods:

DESIGNER DUMMIES

In a previous section, you create a class to represent items in a line of men's clothing. Add fields for the name of the designer and the cost of the item. The designer's name is static because all items in the line come from the same designer — Dummies House of Fashion.

Write code to display eight rows. The first row displays the designer's name. The next six rows describe one complete men's wardrobe. The last row shows the wardrobe's total cost.

COUNT ME IN

In a previous section, you create a class to represent a playing card. Add a static field to your PlayingCard class. The field keeps track of the number of times the class's constructor has been called, and thus has a count of the number of playing cards.

ATTACK OF THE MUTANTS

What's the output of the following code? Make some predictions, and then run the code to see whether your predictions are correct:

package com.example.mutants;

import static java.lang.System.out;

public class Main {

public static void main(String[] args) {

out.println("bigValue: " + MutableInteger.bigValue);
// out.println("bigValue: " + IntegerHolder.value); ILLEGAL

var holder1 = new MutableInteger(42);
var holder2 = new MutableInteger(7);

out.println("holder1: " + holder1.value);
out.println("holder2: " + holder2.value);
out.println();
holder1.value++;
holder2.value++;
MutableInteger.bigValue++;

out.println("bigValue: " + MutableInteger.bigValue);
out.println("holder1: " + holder1.value);
out.println("holder2: " + holder2.value);

out.println();
holder1.bigValue++;
out.println("bigValue according to holder1: " + holder1.bigValue);
out.println("bigValue according to holder2: " + holder2.bigValue);
}
}

class MutableInteger {
int value;
static int bigValue = 1_000_000;

public MutableInteger(int value) {
this.value = value;
}
}

Chapter 12

Using Collections and Streams

IN THIS CHAPTER

Dealing with a bunch of objects at one time

Creating a dictionary

Using Java's cool functional programming features

Developing code for multicore processors

The English word venery means “the act of hunting for wild animals.” In olden times, hunters made up words to refer to collections of animals. For example, a group of birds is a flock, and an assemblage of wolves is a pack. Collective nouns of this kind are called terms of venery. Other examples include a pride of lions, gaggle of geese, school of fish, swarm of bees, herd of cattle, murder of crows, quiver of cobras, convocation of eagles, and litter of cats. (Why anyone would want to go hunting for a bunch of house cats, I'll never know!)

Anyway, Java has many of its own terms of venery. But Java's terms differ from English animals' terms in an important way. Java's terms don't differ from one another by the kinds of things they describe. Instead, they differ in the way the underlying collection is organized. It's like the difference between a committee of people and a mob of people. A mob can be scary, but a committee is usually very boring.

The first part of this chapter is about Java's terms of venery, known to everyone else in the world as Java's collection classes. Once you have collection classes, you can take full advantage of Java's functional programming features. Those functional programming features dominate this chapter's second half.

Using an ArrayList

One of the most commonly used collection classes is the ArrayList. Listing 12-1 shows you how it works.

LISTING 12-1 Working with a Java Collection

import module java.base;

public class ShowAllWords {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

ArrayList<String> vocabulary = new ArrayList<>();

var diskScanner = new Scanner(new File("AllWords.txt"));
while (diskScanner.hasNext()) {
vocabulary.add(diskScanner.nextLine());
}
diskScanner.close();

vocabulary.remove(0);
vocabulary.add(2, "paradox");

for (String word : vocabulary) {
System.out.println(word);
}
}
}

CLEARING THE CLUTTER

You may want to see a punchier, more impactful version of the code in Listing 12-1. If so, here's the simple source file:

void main() throws IOException {

ArrayList<String> vocabulary = new ArrayList<>();

var diskScanner = new Scanner(new File("AllWords.txt"));
while (diskScanner.hasNext()) {
vocabulary.add(diskScanner.nextLine());
}
diskScanner.close();

vocabulary.remove(0);
vocabulary.add(2, "paradox");

for (String word : vocabulary) {
println(word);
}
}

I'm happy to report that this shorter version does everything that the code in Listing 12-1 does. Just remember that this sidebar's code has an implicitly declared class and the ability to create such classes is a preview feature in Java 23. This feature may go away, change, or become official in later versions of Java.

For some advice about using Java's preview features, refer to Chapter 2.

The code in Listing 12-1 reads an AllWords.txt file and loads the file's values in an ArrayList named vocabulary. Figure 12-1 shows you a sample AllWords.txt file. (In case anyone cares, I got the words in this file by asking ChatGPT.) With that particular AllWords.txt file, the output of Listing 12-1 is what you see in Figure 12-2.

According to Figure 12-1, the word at the start of the AllWords.txt file is luminous. So, you may be tempted to say the following: “Immediately after reading the contents of AllWords.txt, the first value in the vocabulary list is the word luminous.” If you say this, you're mostly correct.

Why do I say “mostly correct”? It's because the word first suggests “number 1,” but luminous isn't the “number 1” value in the vocabulary list. Computer languages number everything starting with 0, not 1. Because of this, these statements are true:

  • The index of luminous in the vocabulary list is 0.
  • The index of the next word, harbor, in the vocabulary list is 1.
  • The index of the next word, zephyr, in the vocabulary list is 2.
  • And so on.

See Figure 12-3.

You can guess what happens when Java executes vocabulary.remove(0) in Listing 12-1. The element with index 0 (the word luminous) gets taken from the list. As a result, the word harbor moves to the 0-index slot. In fact, all remaining values move leftward to fill in the gap. After removing luminous from the list, you have the vocabulary list shown in Figure 12-4.

The next statement in Listing 12-1, vocabulary.add(2, "paradox"), inserts the word paradox into the list and gives that word the index 2. Once again, some values in the list get new indices. In particular, the words from enigma onward move over to accommodate the insertion. (See Figure 12-5.)

Notice that an ArrayList instance has two different add methods.

  • The first add method in Listing 12-1 has only one parameter:

    vocabulary.add(diskScanner.nextLine());

    This statement takes whatever word it finds on a line of the input file and appends that word to the end of the list.

  • The second add method in Listing 12-1 has two parameters:

    vocabulary.add(2, "paradox")

    Rather than append a word to the end of the file, this method inserts the word at a specific index in the file.

A new way to do looping

The last few lines of Listing 12-1 contain an enhancedforloop — a for loop that doesn't use counters or indices. An enhanced for loop has three parts:

for (variableType variableName : rangeOfValues)

In Listing 12-1, the variableName is word, and the variableType is String. During each loop iteration, the word variable takes on a new String value. The loop's rangeOfValues is vocabulary. So, during the initial loop iteration, the value of word is the vocabulary list's initial entry, which is "harbor". (Refer to Figure 12-5.) During the next iteration, the value of word is the list's next entry, which is "zephyr". After that comes "paradox". And so on.

Java's enhanced for loop requires a word of caution: Each time through the loop, the variable that steps through the range of values stores a copy of the value in the original range. The variable does not point to the range itself.

For example, if you add an assignment statement that changes the value of word in Listing 12-1, this statement has no effect on any of the values stored in the vocabulary array. To drive this point home, imagine filling the vocabulary list with five words: "Air", "Hi", "More", "A", and "I". Then you execute the following code:

for (var word: vocabulary) {
word += "s";
print(word);
print(" ");
}

println("");

for (var word: vocabulary) {
print(word);
print(" ");
}

The word += "s" statement changes each word value inside the topmost for loop. But that statement doesn't change any of the vocabulary list's entries. So the code's output looks like this:

Airs His Mores As Is
Air Hi More A I

Java has some shortcuts for filling a new ArrayList with values. For example, you can write

ArrayList<String> list =
new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("harbor", "zephyr", "enigma", "echo"));

Or, if you want 100 copies of the word Dummies in a list, you can write

ArrayList<String> dummiesList =
new ArrayList<>(Collections.nCopies(100, "Dummies"));

Import a module in one fell swoop

The code in Listing 12-1 uses several classes from Java's API. My original draft of Listing 12-1 started with all these import declarations:

import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Scanner;

Eventually, I replaced these five lines with only one line: the import module java.base declaration at the top of Listing 12-1.

That import module line can replace most of the other import declarations in this book. In particular, all the declarations that begin with import java.util and import java.io can be replaced with this single import module declaration. The reason is that the packages whose names start with java.util and java.io are all inside the java.base module.

You can import the java.base module at the start of any file, even a file that doesn't need any imports at all. (In rare cases, you can stumble into a class name conflict. That's when you need a class in some other module that has the same name as a class in java.base. In that case, Java tells you that you have a problem, and you can take time to work it all out.)

The import module declaration is a win-win. So why don't you see it in earlier chapters? I held off using it until Chapter 12 for three reasons:

  • The import module feature is new.

    In fact, it's a preview feature in Java 23. I don't think it will disappear in later versions of Java, but I can't be sure of it.

  • Old-fashioned import declarations (without the word module) occur in zillions of Java programs.

    It's good to know how those traditional import declarations work. And finally,

  • I didn't think of using import module declarations until after I wrote Chapters 1–11.

    Don't tell anybody about that.

Using generics

Look again at Listing 12-1, shown earlier, and notice the funky ArrayList declaration:

ArrayList<String> vocabulary = new ArrayList<>();

Each collection class is generified. That ugly-sounding word means that every collection declaration should contain some angle-bracketed stuff, such as <String>. The thing that's sandwiched between < and > tells Java what kinds of values the new collection may contain. For example, in Listing 12-1, the words ArrayList<String> vocabulary tell Java that vocabulary is a bunch of strings. That is, the vocabulary list contains String objects (not Room objects, not Account objects, not Employee objects — nothing other than String objects). So, from that point on, any reference to an item from the vocabulary collection is treated exclusively as a String. If you write

vocabulary.add(new Account());

the compiler coughs up your code and spits it out because an Account (created in Chapter 7) isn't the same as a String. (This coughing and spitting happens even if the compiler has access to the Account class's code — the code in Chapter 7.) But the statement

vocabulary.add("George Gow");

is just fine. Because "George Gow" has type String, the compiler smiles happily.

You have options

For historical reasons, there are a few different ways to define a new collection. For example, if you love typing, you can repeat the generic type name, like so:

ArrayList<String> vocabulary = new ArrayList<String>();

In the right situations, you can use the word var:

var vocabulary = new ArrayList<String>();

You may even see old code that's not generified, like this:

ArrayList vocabulary = new ArrayList();

But I don't recommend writing new declarations this way. Without generics, Java won't know for sure what type of values you're putting into your collection. So the rest of your code may require some special care. For example, you may need extra code to make sure you don't accidentally add an Employee instance or Account instance to your vocabulary list.

Wrap it up

In Chapter 4, I point out that Java has two kinds of types: primitive types and reference types. (If you didn't read those sections, or if you don't remember them, don't feel guilty. You'll be okay.) Things like int, double, char, and boolean are primitive types, and things like String, Employee, ArrayList, and Account are reference types.

The distinction between primitive types and reference types has been a source of contention since Java's birth in 1995. Even now, Oracle's wizards are hatching plans to work around the stickier consequences of having two kinds of types. One of those consequences is that collections, such as the ArrayList, can't contain values of a primitive type. For example, it's okay to write

ArrayList<String> vocabulary = new ArrayList<>();

but it's not okay to write

ArrayList<int> numbers = new ArrayList<>(); // BAD! BAD!

because int is a primitive type. So, if you want to store values like 3, 55, and 21 in an ArrayList, what do you do? Rather than store int values in the ArrayList, you store Java's Integer values:

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();

In previous chapters, you see the Integer class in connection with the parseInt method:

int numberOfCows = Integer.parseInt("536");

The Integer class has many methods, such as parseInt, for dealing with int values. The class also has fields such as MAX_VALUE and MIN_VALUE, which stand for the largest and smallest values that int variables may have.

The Integer class is an example of a wrapper class. Each of Java's eight primitive types has a corresponding wrapper class. You can use methods and fields in Java's Double, Character, Boolean, Long, Float, Short, and Byte wrapper classes. For example, the Double class has methods named parseDouble, compareTo, toHexString, and fields named MAX_VALUE and MAX_EXPONENT.

Notice the pattern. All eight of Java's primitive types (such as int, double, and char) have names that start with lowercase letters. In contrast, all the wrapper classes (Integer, Double, Character, and so on) have names that begin with uppercase letters.

Java programmers like to begin the names of classes with uppercase letters. You can declare public class account or public class employee. But if you do, other programmers will think you're a rube.

The Integer class wraps the primitive int type with useful methods and values. In addition, you can create an Integer instance that wraps a single int value:

Integer myInteger = Integer.valueOf(42);

In this line of code, the myInteger variable has one int value inside it: the int value 42. In Paul's words, wrapping the int value 42 into an Integer object myInteger is “something like putting lots of extra breading on okra — it makes 42 more digestible for finicky eaters like collections.”

Instances of the other wrapper classes work the same way. For example, an instance of the Double class wraps up a single primitive double value:

Double averageNumberOfTomatoes = Double.valueOf(1.41421356237);

Here's a program that stores five Integer values in an ArrayList:

void main() {
ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
fillTheList(list);
for (Integer n : list) {
println(n);
}
}

public static void fillTheList(ArrayList<Integer> list) {
list.add(85);
list.add(19);
list.add(0);
list.add(103);
list.add(13);
}

In the code, notice calls like list.add(85) that have int value parameters. At this point, little Billy gets excited and says, “Look, Mom! I added the primitive int value 85 to my ArrayList!” No, Billy. That's not what's going on.

In this code, the list collection contains Integer values, not int values. A primitive int value is a lot like an instance of the Integer class. But a primitive int value isn't exactly the same as an Integer instance.

What's going on is called autoboxing. Before Java 5.0, you had to write

list.add(new Integer(85));

if you wanted to add an Integer to an ArrayList. But Java 5.0 and later Java versions can automatically wrap an int value inside a box. An int value in a parameter list becomes an Integer in ArrayList. Java's autoboxing feature makes programs easier to read and write.

Are we done yet?

Here's a pleasant surprise. When you write a program like the one shown previously, in Listing 12-1, you don't have to know how many names are in the input file. Having to know the number of names may defeat the purpose of using the easily expandable ArrayList class. Rather than loop until you read exactly nine names, you can loop until you run out of data.

The Scanner class has several nice methods, such as hasNextInt, hasNextDouble, and plain old hasNext. Each of these methods checks for more input data. If there's more data, the method returns true. Otherwise, the method returns false.

Listing 12-1 uses the general-purpose hasNext method. This hasNext method returns true as long as there's anything more to read from the program's input. After the program scoops up that last driftwood line in Figure 12-1, the subsequent hasNext call returns false. This false condition ends execution of the while loop and plummets the computer toward the remainder of the Listing 12-1 code.

The hasNext method is quite handy. In fact, hasNext is so handy that it's part of a bigger concept known as an iterator, and iterators are baked into all of Java's collection classes.

Once and again

An iterator spits out a collection's values, one after another. To obtain a value from the collection, you call the iterator's next method. To find out whether the collection has any more values in it, you call the iterator's hasNext method. For example, you can replace the loop at the end of Listing 12-1 with the following code:

Iterator<String> iterator = vocabulary.iterator();
while (iterator.hasNext()) {
System.out.println(iterator.next());
}

The first line of code creates an iterator from the vocabulary collection. The second and third lines call the iterator's hasNext and next methods to grab all objects stored in the vocabulary collection — one for each iteration of the loop. These lines display each of the vocabulary collection's values. When you make this code replacement, you get the same output as before. (You get the output in Figure 12-2.)

To run this code, you may need an import java.util.Iterator declaration.

Which is better? An enhanced for loop or an iterator? Java programmers prefer the enhanced for loop because the for loop involves less baggage — no iterator object to carry from one line of code to the next. But as you can see later in this chapter, the most programming-enhanced feature can be upgraded, streamlined, tweaked, and otherwise reconstituted. There's no end to the way you can improve upon your code.

Sorting and Searching

Every introductory computer programming book has sections featuring two important problems:

  • Sorting: Reorder the values in a list from increasing to decreasing, or from decreasing to increasing.
  • Searching: Find a particular value that's one of many values in a list. Report the location of that value in the list.

Java has methods to solve both of these problems easily. You can see them in Listing 12-2.

LISTING 12-2 Where in the World Is the Word “Enigma”?

void main() throws IOException {
ArrayList<String> vocabulary = new ArrayList<>();

var diskScanner = new Scanner(new File("AllWords.txt"));
while (diskScanner.hasNext()) {
vocabulary.add(diskScanner.nextLine());
}
diskScanner.close();

Collections.sort(vocabulary);
for (String word : vocabulary) {
println(word);
}

println("");
print("Enigma's index: ");
println(vocabulary.indexOf("enigma"));
}

Figure 12-6 shows a run of the code in Listing 12-2.

In Listing 12-2, the call Collections.sort(vocabulary) rearranges the values in the vocabulary list. This call uses the default arrangement, which is alphabetical ordering.

Later in Listing 12-2, the call vocabulary.indexOf("enigma") returns the index of the first occurrence of the word "enigma" in the sorted vocabulary list. In Figure 12-6, driftwood has index 0, echo has index 1, and enigma has index 2. And, sure enough, a call to indexOf("enigma") returns the 2 that you see at the end of Figure 12-6.

Java's sorting methods are versatile. You can arrange values in any order you want. For example, the call Collections.reverse(vocabulary) arranges an alphabetically sorted list in reverse alphabetical order. And the call

Collections.sort(vocabulary, Comparator.comparingInt(w -> w.charAt(w.length() - 1)));

arranges values based on the last letter in each word.

Chapter 11 describes Java's static keyword and reveals some of the things you do when you bump into a static field or method. In Listing 12-1, you write Collections.sort because sort is a static method in Java's Collections class. My college students freeze up when I use the word static. So, if you don't understand this paragraph, don't worry about it. You can learn about static as you write more Java programs.

Another Kind of Collection Class

I tried to find out how many collection classes the Java 23 API has, but I gave up after a while. It has too many for a simple tally. Anyway, I decided to show off a class whose structure differs significantly from the ArrayList class. It's Java's HashMap class.

A HashMap instance stores a lookup table. For example, Dr. Rachael Tatman counted the number of occurrences of 333,333 words on Internet pages and published her results at www.kaggle.com/datasets/rtatman/english-word-frequency . I copied ten of her values to create a file named WordFrequencies.txt. (In retrospect, I should have asked her to count the number of collection classes in Java's API!) My WordFrequencies.txt file is shown in Figure 12-7.

The code in Listing 12-3 reads the WordFrequencies.txt file into a hash map. Then the program tries to find two words in the hash map and output those numbers' frequencies.

LISTING 12-3 Using a HashMap

void main() throws IOException {
var diskScanner = new Scanner(new File("WordFrequencies.txt"));

var map = new HashMap<String, Integer>();

while (diskScanner.hasNext()) {
map.put(diskScanner.next(), diskScanner.nextInt());
}
diskScanner.close();

println(map.get("quicksilver"));
println(map.get("dummies"));
}

For a run of the code in Listing 12-3, see Figure 12-8.

Listing 12-3 creates a variable whose type is HashMap<String, Integer>. So the map is shaped like a 2-column table, with String values in the first column and Integer values in the second column. It's the same shape as the text in Figure 12-7. (If you're not sure why the type declaration says <String, Integer> instead of <String, int>, refer to this chapter's earlier section “Wrap it up.”)

The most important methods in the HashMap class are put and get. You call put to add a row to the map and get to fetch a value from the map.

For example, the loop in Listing 12-3 fills the map by calling put several times. Each time, the call's parameters are a String value (like the word "luminous"), and an Integer value (like the number 1521841). When the loop is finished reading the file in Figure 12-7, the map variable's HashMap instance has ten word/number pairs.

To find out how many times Dr. Tatman found the word quicksilver, you call map.get("quicksilver") near the end of Listing 12-3. According to Figure 12-8, she found quicksilver 808,862 times.

The last statement in Listing 12-3 looks for the frequency of the word dummies. In fact, Dr. Tatman's research saw the word dummies 3,392,894 times, but I didn't put that information in my WordFrequencies.txt file. So Listing 12-3 doesn't add "dummies" to the program's hash map. As a result, the call to map.get("dummies") returns nothing at all. And, in Java, the word null means “nothing at all.”

So many collection classes!

The ArrayList class that I use in many of this chapter's examples is only the tip of the Java collections iceberg. The Java library contains many collections classes, each with its own advantages. Table 12-1 contains an abbreviated list.

To find out which collection classes best meet your needs, visit https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Collection.html. (Warning: This page is difficult to read!)

Once again, I'd like to put you to work:

OUR BEST PLAYERS

Use the Player class from Chapter 11 to make an ArrayList of Player objects. Write a program to display the names of the players whose average is .100 or higher.

OUR BIGGEST NUMBER

Create an ArrayList containing Integer values. Then step through the values in the list to find the largest value among all values in the list. For example, if the list contains the numbers 85, 19, 0, 103, and 13, display the number 103.

INSERT IN ORDER

Create an ArrayList containing String values in alphabetical order. When the user types an additional word on the keyboard, the program inserts the new word into the ArrayList in the proper (alphabetically ordered) place.

For example, imagine that the list starts off containing the words "cat", "dog", "horse", and "zebra" (in that order). After the user types the word fish on the keyboard (and presses Enter), the list contains the words "cat", "dog", "fish", "horse", and "zebra" (in that order).

To write this program, you may find the String class's compareToIgnoreCase method and the ArrayList class's size method useful. You can find out about these methods by visiting https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/String.html#compareToIgnoreCase(java.lang.String) and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/ArrayList.html#size().

A REAL DICTIONARY

Modify the code in Listing 12-3 so that the map contains ten words and their definitions. When the user types one of the ten words, the program displays that word's definition.

Functional Programming

From 1953 to 1957, John Backus and others developed the FORTRAN programming language, which contained the basic framework for thousands of today's programming languages. The framework has come to be known as imperative programming because of its do-this-then-do-that nature.

A few years after the rise of FORTRAN, John McCarthy created another language, named Lisp. Unlike FORTRAN, the underlying framework for Lisp is functional programming. In a purely functional program, you avoid writing “do this, then do that.” Instead, you write things like “Here's how you'll be transforming this into that when you get around to doing the transformation.”

For one reason or another, imperative programming became the dominant mode. But in recent years, functional programming has emerged as a powerful and useful way of thinking about code.

Problem-solving the old-fashioned way

Congratulations! Your license to sell goods over the Internet has been approved. You've set up an e-commerce site and paid for some advertising. Your inventory includes joke books and novelty prank toys. One of the toys is a can with a label that says Cashew Nuts. When someone opens it, a fake, spring-loaded snake pops out. Another of your toys is a small buzzer. When you shake someone's hand, you surprise them with a fast vibration. You also sell traditional Groucho eyeglasses. Whoever wears them appears to have bushy eyebrows and a big mustache.

In your world, the sale of a single item looks something like the stuff in Listing 12-4. Each sale has an item and a price.

LISTING 12-4 The Sale Class

package com.example.sales;

public record Sale(String item, double price) {
}

To make use of the Sale class, you create a small program. The program totals up the sales on books. The program is shown in Listing 12-5.

LISTING 12-5 Total Sales of Books

import com.example.sales.Sale;

void main() {
ArrayList<Sale> sales = new ArrayList<>();
var currency = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance();

fillTheList(sales);

double runningTotal = 0;
for (Sale sale : sales) {
if (itemIsBook(sale)) {
runningTotal += sale.price();
}
}
println(currency.format(runningTotal));
}

boolean itemIsBook(Sale sale) {
return sale.item().equals("Book");
}

void fillTheList(ArrayList<Sale> sales) {
sales.add(new Sale("Book", 10.95));
sales.add(new Sale("Book", 30.00));
sales.add(new Sale("Toy", 9.67));
sales.add(new Sale("Book", 20.00));
}

The output of the program in Listing 12-5 is $60.95. That's the total revenue from all books sold. On my computer, the combination of

var currency = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance();

and

currency.format(runningTotal)

makes that total look like a US dollar amount.

You can customize the display for your own country's currency. For example, with the code

var currency = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.JAPAN);

the program's output is ¥61.

A familiar problem

The scenario in Listing 12-5 isn't unusual. You have a collection of items (a collection of sales, perhaps). You step through the items in the collection, finding the items that meet certain criteria (the sale of a book, for example). You grab a certain value (such as the sale price) of each item that meets your criteria. Then you do something useful with the values you've grabbed (for example, adding the values together).

Here are some other examples:

  • Step through your list of employees. Find each employee whose performance evaluation scored 3 or higher. Give each such employee a $100 bonus and then determine the total amount of money you'll pay in bonuses.
  • Step through your list of customers. For each customer who has shown interest in buying a smartphone, send the customer an email about this month's discount plans.
  • Step through the list of planets that have been discovered. For each M-class planet, find the probability of finding intelligent life on that planet. Then find the average of all such probabilities.

This scenario is so common that it's worth finding better and better ways to deal with the scenario. One way to deal with it is to use some of the functional programming features in Java.

Lambda expressions

In Chapter 3 of Java For Dummies, the author says,

In Java, a method is a list of things to do. Every method has a name, and you tell the computer to do the things in the list by using the method's name in your program.

He's a clever fellow because, in this sentence, he's careful to use the word method. Yes, a method is a list of things to do, but not all to-do lists are methods, and not all to-do lists have names.

A lambda expression is a to-do list with no name. Here's an example:

sale -> sale.item().equals("Book")

When you put this expression in just the right place, the expression does the work of the itemIsBook method in Listing 12-5. Figure 12-9 brings this point home.

A lambda expression is a concise way of creating a list of things to do. The list may include only one to-do item (as in Figure 12-9) or any number of items:

sale -> {
var compareTo = "Book";
return sale.item().equals(compareTo);
}

When you put more than one to-do item in a lambda expression, the expression must have a complete method body with curly braces, semicolons, and the return keyword. Only the stuff before the arrow (->) is abbreviated.

The lambda expression in Figure 12-9 has only one parameter: the sale parameter. Can a lambda expression have more than one parameter? Of course, it can. Here's an example:

(price1, price2) -> price1 + price2

When you have more than one parameter, you have to surround the parameters with parentheses and separate them with commas.

Figure 12-10 describes the new lambda expression's meaning.

The lambda expression in Figure 12-10 does (roughly) what the following method does:

double sum(double price1, double price2) {
return price1 + price2;
}

The interpretation of streams

The earlier section “Once and again” introduces iterators. An iterator's next method spits out a collection's values, one by one. That's helpful, but Java takes this concept a step further with the notion of a stream. A stream is like an iterator except that, with a stream, you don't have to call a next method. A stream spits out a collection's values automatically. To get values from a stream, you don't call a stream's next method. Instead, you create a pipeline that pulls values from the stream. This pipeline solution uses concepts from functional programming.

A pipeline consists of several methods. Each method takes the data, transforms the data in some way or another, and hands its results to the next method in line. Figure 12-11 illustrates the pipeline for this chapter's sales problem.

In Figure 12-11, imagine a bunch of raw materials as they're transformed along an assembly line. Each downward-pointing arrow in the figure represents a method (or, metaphorically, a worker on the assembly line).

For example, in the transition from the figure's second box to the third box, a worker method (the filter method) sifts out sales of items that aren't books. Imagine Lucy Ricardo (in the classic “I Love Lucy” episode at the chocolate factory) standing between the second and third boxes, removing each toy from the assembly line and tossing it carelessly onto the floor.

Taken as a whole, the entire pipeline shown in Figure 12-11 adds up the prices of books sold. Listing 12-6 contains a complete program using the streams and lambda expressions of Figure 12-11.

LISTING 12-6 Living the Functional Way of Life

import com.example.sales.Sale;

void main() {
ArrayList<Sale> sales = new ArrayList<>();
var currency = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance();

fillTheList(sales);

double total = sales.stream()
.filter(sale -> sale.item().equals("Book"))
.map(sale -> sale.price())
.reduce(0.0, (price1, price2) -> price1 + price2);

println(currency.format(total));
}

void fillTheList(ArrayList<Sale> sales) {
sales.add(new Sale("Book", 10.95));
sales.add(new Sale("Book", 30.00));
sales.add(new Sale("Toy", 9.67));
sales.add(new Sale("Book", 20.00));
}

The output of the program in Listing 12-6 is $60.95 (the same as the output of Listing 12-5).

The boldface code in Listing 12-6 is one big Java assignment statement. The stuff after the equal sign is a sequence of method calls. Each method call passes items to the next method call in line. That's how you form the pipeline.

The next few sections describe each of the method calls.

Getting a stream from a collection

When you do functional programming in Java, you start with a collection and call the stream method on that collection. This gives you a stream that feeds items from the collection to the rest of the code's pipeline. For example, in Listing 12-6, the name sales refers to an ArrayList, and sales.stream() refers to a stream. (See Figure 12-12.)

Filtering the items in a stream

A filter method takes items from one stream and passes some of them to another stream. The filter method's parameter is a condition, and the items that get passed are the ones that satisfy the condition. For example, in Listing 12-6, the lambda expression

sale -> sale.item().equals("Book")

returns true for a particular sale item as long as that sale happens to be a book.

Figure 12-13 illustrates the work of the filter method in Listing 12-6.

Getting a value from each item in a stream

A map method takes each item in a stream, does something with that item, and then passes the “something” to the next stream in the pipeline. For example, with each sale, the map method in Listing 12-6 gets the price of the sale and passes that price onward.

Figure 12-14 illustrates the work of the map method in Listing 12-6.

Summarizing the items in a stream

A reduce method combines a stream's items. The reduce call in Listing 12-6 adds all the values from its incoming stream — the stream that comes from the map method. That incoming stream has the prices of all the books from the original sales list. (See Figure 12-15.)

Java's reduce method does more than just scrunch numbers together. The method takes two parameters:

  • The first parameter is an initial value.

    In Figure 12-15, the initial value is 0.0.

  • The second parameter is a function (usually, a lambda expression) that takes two of its own parameters and returns yet another value. For example, in Figure 12-15, the lambda expression takes two parameters, price1 and price2, and returns the sum:

    (price1, price2) -> price1 + price2

The lambda expression combines the values from the incoming stream. The initial value serves as the starting point for all the combining. So, in Figure 12-15, the reduce method performs three additions. (See Figure 12-16.)

For comparison, imagine calling the method

reduce(10.0, (value1, value2) -> value1 * value2)

with the stream whose values include 3.0, 2.0, and 5.0. The resulting action is shown in Figure 12-17.

The reduce method plays a special role in Listing 12-6. Every method in a stream performs a kind of operation: either an intermediate operation or a terminal operation. An intermediate operation is one that returns another stream. A terminal operation is one that either returns something other than a stream or returns nothing (void).

A chain of calls like the one in Listing 12-6 begins with one or more intermediate operations and ends with a single terminal operation. For example, in Listing 12-6, filter and map perform intermediate operations, and reduce performs a terminal operation. In a sense, the terminal operation pulls values from all the intermediate operations. When Java tries to find the value of total, the terminal reduce operation eagerly asks for price1 and price2. At that moment, the lazy, intermediate filter and map operations wake up and start pumping out values.

If you don't put a terminal operation call at the end of your call chain, Java doesn't execute any of the intermediate calls. For an example, see the Try It Out paragraph at the end of this chapter.

Why bother?

The chain of method calls in Listing 12-6 accomplishes everything that the loop in Listing 12-5 accomplishes. But the code in Figure 12-14 uses concepts from functional programming. What's the big deal? Are you better off with Listing 12-6 than with Listing 12-5?

You are. For the past several years, the big trend in chip design has been multicore processors. With several cores, a processor can execute several statements at the same time, speeding up a program's execution by a factor of 2 or 4 or 8 or even more. Programs run much faster if you divide the work among several cores. But how do you divide the work?

You can modify the imperative code in Listing 12-5. For example, with some fancy features, you can hand different loop iterations to different cores. But the resulting code is messy. For the code to work properly, you have to micromanage the loop iterations, checking carefully to make sure that the final runningTotal value is correct.

In contrast, the functional code is easy to modify. To take advantage of multicore processors, you change only one word in Listing 12-6!

double total = sales.parallelStream()
.filter(sale -> sale.item().equals("Book"))
.map(sale -> sale.price())
.reduce(0.0, (price1, price2) -> price1 + price2);

In Listing 12-6, the stream() method call creates a serial stream. With a serial stream, Java does its processing one sale at a time. But a call to parallelStream() creates a slightly different kind of stream: a parallel stream. With a parallel stream, Java divides the work among the number of cores in the computer's processor (or according to some other useful measure of computing power). If you have 4 million sales and four cores, each core processes 1 million of the sales.

Each core works independently of the others, and each core dumps its result into a final reduce method. The reduce method combines the cores' results into a final tally. In the best possible scenario, all the work gets done in one-fourth the time it would take with an ordinary serial stream.

When you read the preceding paragraph, don't gloss over the phrase best possible scenario. Parallelism isn't magic. And sometimes, parallelism isn't your friend. Consider the situation in which you have only 20 sale amounts to tally. The time it takes to divide the problem into four groups of 5 sales each far exceeds the amount of time you save in using all four cores. In addition, some problems don't lend themselves to parallel processing. Imagine that the price of an item depends on the number of similar items being sold. In that case, you can't divide the problem among four independently operating cores. If you try, each core has to know what the other cores are doing. You lose the advantage of having four threads of execution.

NO VARIABLES? NO PROBLEM!

In imperative programming, your code's pieces interact with one another. All the pieces might be updating the current price of Oracle stock shares (ticker symbol: ORCL). The simultaneous updates may conflict with one another and result in an incorrect outcome. You've experienced the same phenomenon if you've ever clicked a website's Purchase button, only to learn that the item you're trying to purchase is out of stock. Someone else completed a purchase while you were filling in your credit card information. Too many customers were grabbing for the same goods at the same time.

The source of the problem is shared data. How many clients share simultaneous access to Oracle's stock price? How many customers share access to a web page's Purchase button? Today's multicore processors can perform more than one instruction at a time. How many simultaneous instructions can all be trying to modify the same variable's value?

In imperative programming, a variable is a place where statements share their values with one another. Can you avoid using variables in your code?

Compare the loop in Listing 12-5 with the functional programming code in Listing 12-6. In Listing 12-5, the runningTotal variable is shared among all loop iterations. Because each iteration can potentially change the value of runningTotal, you can't assign each iteration to a different processor core. If you did, you'd risk having two cores updating that running total at the same time. (Chances are good that, because of the simultaneous updating, neither core would do its update correctly!) But the filter/map/reduce lines in Listing 12-6 make no reference to the code's total variable. The program's total variable is a final tally, not a running total. In fact, none of the variables in Listing 12-6 represents a running total. In Listing 12-6, the running total is completely anonymous.

In imperative programming, a variable is a place where statements share their values with one another. But functional programming shuns variables. So, when you do functional programming, you don't have a lot of data sharing. Many of the difficulties associated with shared data vanish into thin air.

Here's an analogy: Imagine a programming problem as a cube, and then imagine an imperative programming solution as a way of slicing the cube into manageable pieces. (See the first sidebar figure.)

To get the most out of a four-core processor, you divide your code into four pieces — one piece for each core. But with imperative programming, your program's pieces don't fit neatly into your processor's cores. The figure shows what happens when you try to squeeze an imperative program into a multicore processor.

Functional programming also divides code into pieces, but it does so along different lines. With functional programming, the pieces of the code fit neatly into the processor's cores. (See the second sidebar figure.)

Functional code eliminates much of the worry about sharing data among the parts of a program. In that way, functional programming is an elegant solution to an important computing problem.

Method references

Take a critical look at the last lambda expression in Listing 12-6:

(price1, price2) -> price1 + price2)

This expression does roughly the same work as a sum method. (In fact, you can find a sum method's declaration in the earlier section “Lambda expressions.”) If your choice is between typing a 3-line sum method and typing a 1-line lambda expression, you'll probably choose the lambda expression. But what if you have a third alternative? Rather than type your own sum method, you can refer to an existing sum method. Using an existing method is the quickest and safest thing to do.

As luck would have it, Java's Double class contains a static sum method. You don't have to create your own sum method. If you run the following code:

double i = 5.0, j = 7.0;
println(Double.sum(i, j));

the computer displays 12.0. So, rather than type the price1 + price2 lambda expression in Listing 12-6, you can use two colons to create a method reference — an expression that refers to an existing method.

sales.stream()
.filter(sale -> sale.item().equals("Book"))
.map(sale -> sale.price())
.reduce(0.0, Double :: sum);

The expression Double :: sum refers to the sum method belonging to Java's Double class. When you use this Double :: sum method reference, you do the same thing that the last lambda expression does in Listing 12-6. Everybody is happy.

For information about static methods, see Chapter 11.

Some black sheep among the lambdas

In this chapter, I've saved the worst for last. I refuse to give the following code a listing number. Instead, I refer to it as the “Ugly Code.”

UGLY CODE: Lambda Expressions with Side Effects

// This code works correctly, but its style is terrible.

import com.example.sales.Sale;

double runningTotal = 0.0;

void main() {
ArrayList<Sale> sales = new ArrayList<>();
var currency = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance();

fillTheList(sales);

var kindOfItem = "Book";

sales.stream()
.filter(sale -> sale.item().equals(kindOfItem))
.map(sale -> sale.price())
.forEach(price -> addToRunningTotal(price));


println(currency.format(runningTotal));
}

void addToRunningTotal(double price) {
runningTotal += price;
}

void fillTheList(ArrayList<Sale> sales) {
sales.add(new Sale("Book", 10.95));
sales.add(new Sale("Book", 30.00));
sales.add(new Sale("Toy", 9.67));
sales.add(new Sale("Book", 20.00));
}

The forEach method in this ugly code does what its name suggests. It executes its lambda expression for every sale that comes its way. The ugly code uses forEach to tally up the prices of all book sales.

The output of this code is the same as the code in Listings 12-5 and 12-6. But there's more to writing code than getting the correct output. Figure 12-18 compares the three lambda expressions in the ugly code's stream.

Functional programming enthusiasts like the middle expression in Figure 12-18 — the sale -> sale.price() expression. That expression gets information from its parameter (sale) and returns a value (the price of that sale) to the rest of the code.

Functional programmers don't like the other two expressions in Figure 12-18. That's because the other two expressions have side effects. A side effect takes place when a method or lambda expression refers to a value other than a parameter or its return value.

Side effects make programs difficult to understand. Programs without side effects have fewer bugs than programs with side effects. So, in functional programming, a side effect is considered a second-class citizen, a last resort, a tactic you use when you can't simply take in a parameter and return a result.

You can always try the programming challenges that you dream up on your own. If you have no ideas to give you practice with functional programming, I have a couple of suggestions for you:

BE GENEROUS

Each employee has a name and a performance evaluation score. Find the total amount of money you'll pay in bonuses if you give a $100 bonus to each employee whose score is 3 or higher. In your code, make optimal use of lambda expressions and method references.

SAVE TIME

Each recipe has a name, a list of ingredients (some of which involve meat products), and an estimated preparation time. Find the average time estimate for cooking one of the vegetarian recipes.

INTERMEDIATE METHODS ARE JUST PLAIN LAZY

In the earlier section “The interpretation of streams,” I warn that Java does nothing when you end a chain without a terminal operation. To double-check that I'm not lying about this, run the following code:

void main() {
ArrayList<String> words =
new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("I", "am", "happy."));

var sentence = words.stream()
.peek(word -> println(word))
.reduce("", (word1, word2) -> word1 + " " + word2);

println(sentence);
}

The lambda expression in Java's peek method never returns a value. So, aside from executing the lambda expression, peek doesn't modify the stream in any way. The peek method simply passes the stream's values on to the next method in line.

But peek performs an intermediate operation — not a terminal operation. So rerun the code with the following changes. You'll find out what happens when you end a chain with an intermediate operation:

var sentence = words.stream()
.peek(word -> println(word));
// .reduce("", (word1, word2) -> word1 + " " + word2);

// println(sentence);

STREAMLESS VARMINT

You don't need streams to make use of Java's lambda expressions. Run this code for a glimpse at the possibilities:

void main() {
println(change("Hello", string -> {return string + "!";}));
}

String change(String str, Function<String, String> func) {
return func.apply(str);
}

Chapter 13

Using Arrays to Juggle Values

IN THIS CHAPTER

Dealing with several values at a time

Writing to disk files

Running a program with different values each time

Welcome to the Java Motel! No haughty bellhops, no overpriced room service, none of the silly jokes that I write in other chapters. Just a nice room at a darn good price!

Getting Your Ducks All in a Row

The Java Motel, with its ten comfortable rooms, sits in a quiet place off the main highway. Aside from a small, separate office, the motel is just one long row of ground-floor rooms. Each room is easily accessible from the spacious front parking lot.

Oddly enough, the motel’s rooms are numbered 0 through 9. I could say that the numbering is a fluke — something to do with the builder’s original design plan. But the truth is that starting with 0 makes the examples in this chapter easier to write. Computer programming structures start counting from 0 onward. That's all there is to it.

Anyway, you’re trying to keep track of the number of guests in each room. To store all the numbers, you use an array.

An array is a row of values, like the row of rooms in a 1-floor motel. To picture the array, look at the Java Motel in Figure 13-1.

In the lingo of this chapter, the entire row of rooms is called an array. Each room in the array is called a component of the array (also known as an array element). Each component has two numbers associated with it:

  • The room number (a number from 0 to 9), which is called an index of the array
  • A number of guests, which is a value stored in a component of the array

To declare an array with ten int values in it, you can write one fairly short statement:

int[] guests = new int[10];

If your declaration is inside of a method, you can use var, like so:

var guests = new int[10];

In some situations, it's handy to create an array in two separate steps, like this:

class MyClass {

int[] guests; // The var keyword isn't permitted here.

void myMethod() {
guests = new int[10]; // This must be inside a method body.
// …
}

// …
}

In each of these code snippets, notice the use of the number 10. This number tells the computer to make the guests array have ten components. Each component of the array has a name of its own. The starting component is named guests[0], the next is named guests[1], and so on. The last of the ten components is named guests[9].

A declaration like

int[] guests;

doesn't reserve any space to store int values. It only reserves the variable name guests to eventually refer to an array of int values;

In an array declaration, you can put the square brackets before or after the variable name. In other words, you can write int[] guests or int guests[]. Java creates the same guests variable no matter which form you use.

How to book hotel guests

Business is booming at the Java Motel. (Most people prefer the Java Motel over its competitor — the C-Side Resort and Motor Lodge.) As the Java Motel's owner, manager, and system administrator, you have a file containing the number of guests in each room. A sample file named GuestList.txt is shown in Figure 13-2.

After you've made a file, you can call on the Scanner class to get values from the file. The code is shown in Listing 13-1, and the resulting output is in Figure 13-3.

For tips on reading from disk files, refer to Chapter 9.

LISTING 13-1 Filling an Array with Values

import module java.base;

public class ShowGuests {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
int[] guests = new int[10];
var diskScanner = new Scanner(new File("GuestList.txt"));

for (int roomNum = 0; roomNum < 10; roomNum++) {
guests[roomNum] = diskScanner.nextInt();
}

diskScanner.close();

System.out.println("Room\tGuests");
for (int roomNum = 0; roomNum < 10; roomNum++) {
System.out.print(roomNum);
System.out.print("\t");
System.out.println(guests[roomNum]);
}
}
}

The code in Listing 13-1 has two for loops: The first loop reads numbers of guests, and the second loop writes numbers of guests.

Tab stops and other special things

In Listing 13-1, some calls to print and println use the \t escape sequence. It's called an escape sequence because you escape from displaying the letter t on the screen. Instead, the characters \t stand for a tab. The computer moves forward to the next tab stop before printing any more characters. Java has a few of these handy escape sequences. Some of them are shown in Table 13-1.

Figure 13-3 looks good because I ran the program in a Mac Terminal window. In the Windows command prompt and Macintosh Terminal, tab stops are eight spaces apart. But in some environments, tab stops are only four spaces apart. With four-space stops, you don't see the sensible alignment that appears earlier, in Figure 13-3. If you want the columns to align no matter where your program runs, replace the tab characters with blank spaces in Listing 13-1. (Of course, if you're fussy, you have to check for numbers with more than one digit. But that's another story.)

Make life easy for yourself

Besides what you see in Listing 13-1, you have another way to fill an array in Java: with an array initializer. When you use an array initializer, you don't even have to tell the computer how many components the array has. The computer figures it out for you.

Here's another trick: You can also use Java's enhanced for loop (from Chapter 12) to step through an array. Listing 13-2 has an array initializer and an enhanced for loop.

LISTING 13-2 Short and Sweet Code!

void main() {
int[] guests = {1, 4, 2, 0, 2, 1, 4, 3, 0, 2};

println("Room\tGuests");

int roomNum = 0;
for (int numGuests : guests) {
print(roomNum++);
print("\t");
println(numGuests);
}
}

Listing 13-2 produces the same output as Listing 13-1, and Listing 13-2 is much easier to read. So why would anyone bother with the code in Listing 13-1? There are several reasons:

  • Putting data in a program, as I do in Listing 13-2, is seldom a good idea.

    Time goes by. Hotel guests come and go. In this chapter's later “Writing to a file” section, you find out how to change the numbers in the GuestList.txt file. That's okay because people write to files all the time. But changing the numbers in Listing 13-2 would be another story. No one wants to edit a Java program whenever a hotel guest arrives or leaves.

  • Array initializers aren't versatile.

    There's a good reason for calling them initializers. You can use this feature to initialize an array (as in Listing 13-2), but you can't use it to assign values to an existing array variable. For example, the initialization in Listing 13-2 is fine and dandy. But the following code is worthy of a slap on the wrist:

    // Bad code:
    int[] guests;
    guests = {1, 4, 2, 0, 2, 1, 4, 3, 0, 2};

  • An enhanced forloop, like the one in Listing 13-2, doesn't track the array's indices.

    In Listing 13-1, both loops have a counter variable named roomNum. That makes it easy to print a room number on each line in the output. (Refer to Figure 13-3.)

    But an enhanced for loop doesn't have its own counter variable. To print the value of roomNum in Listing 13-2, you have to create your own roomNum variable and remember to update it each time through the loop. It's only a tiny amount of extra work. But, in a complicated program, this extra work makes it easier to make a mistake. (I know. I've made those mistakes.)

  • The code in Listing 13-1 is a traditional Java main method. In comparison, the code in Listing 13-2 is a simple source file.

    That makes Listing 13-1 more verbose than Listing 13-2.

    So, why should you have to wade through the public class ShowGuests { public static blah, blah … business in Listing 13-1? One reason is that most Java main methods are written that way. In fact, before Java 21, all of Java's main methods were written that way. That's almost 30 years of Java code with lengthy, long-winded main methods. I can't write a Java book without highlighting some of those main methods.

SPELL IT BACKWARD

Modify the code in Listing 13-1 so that it displays the rooms in reverse room-number order (starting with Room 9 and working down to Room 0).
